notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1250.tmp1250.opp-lat: Line 1: the printed 'Quidem duos homines' is read as 'Quidam duos dominos' ('some [take] the two masters'). 'non ideo timet' is obscure and rendered literally. The sentence 'Omne quodcunque plus diligit homo, hoc est avarus, aurum Deum habet...' seems corrupt; [is his god] is supplied from the parallel sentence later in the passage. Line 3: 'homo malus sit apud Deum quam angeli' is read as 'melior' (man 'better' than the angels), which the argument requires. 'illa enim si laesa fuerit anima, corpus interibit' is rendered as printed; the sense may be that for birds soul and body perish together. Line 4: in the quotation of God's words to Solomon, the edition repeats 'ad discernendum bonum et malum, ecce dedi tibi sapientiam', apparently by dittography; the repeated words are kept in the translation. 'variettte vestro' is read as 'varietate vestium'. 'medio claritate' is read as 'media caritate' (Song of Songs 3:10). 'more sapientis' is read as 'in ore sapientis' (Proverbs 21:20).

Line 5: 'a vobis a constitutione mundi' is as printed; Rev. 13:8 has no 'a vobis', and the text may be corrupt (perhaps for 'ab origine'). 'offertus' (marked 'Ita Cod.') is taken as 'oblatus', 'offered'. 'quantum Christus' is obscure; rendered literally. Line 6: 'et Deus erat apud Deum' looks like a dittography within the quotation of John 1:1; translated as printed. 'quam me' (Ita Cod.) is taken as 'than I'. 'ut dedignaris' is read as 'how do you disdain'. The final sentence, 'just as priests in the Church now do', seems to mean that priests too baptize with water while God alone forgives sins.

Line 8: 'quid est Spiritus sanctus' read as 'quid est [quod] Spiritus sanctus'; 'quærit, illum' read as 'quærite illum'. Line 9: 'Hoc noverat' must mean 'this he did not know' (cf. 'Hoc nesciebat' below); 'oro quo' read as 'pro quo'. 'Sive bonus, sive malus baptizet in ministerio in potestate' appears defective; the sense (cf. Augustine) is that the minister baptizes in ministry, Christ in power. Line 10: 'It;.. teres' read as 'Veteres'; 'speruit' as 'spernit'. Line 11: the definition of 'saeculum' ('quem solem... appellant') and the sentence 'Filii autem regni ejicientur in tenebras exteriores' sit awkwardly and may be corrupt or displaced; 'fornicationum' read as 'fornicationi'; the final quotation breaks off at 'in', supplied as '[you]'.

12: 'in meet.' read as 'in mente'. 'Quod Apostolus faciebat' is translated as it stands, but the sense requires 'non faciebat' (the Apostle did not do this); the text may be corrupt. 'bona pleniter in fide' probably stands for 'beneplacita in fide' in the threefold series. 13: 'Potest in adversos superbos Romanos' is read as 'Potest [et] adversus ... [intellegi]'. 'Et hic dicit' is odd and may be corrupt. 14: 'tantam accipit lonum Spiritum sermo sapientiæ' appears to have lost words. It is read as 'tantum accipit donum. Alii datur per Spiritum sermo sapientiae'. 16: 'ductus' read as 'doctus'.

Editorial apparatus in the printed text has been left out of the translation: '(Ita cod.)' after superinsedunt; '[Cod., fratribus]' after fratrum; '[Cod., cibi tantis]' after convivii exultantis (the manuscript reading is corrupt; the last phrase follows Mai's emendation). 'cant tuam' read as carnem tuam (Isa. 58:7); 'irrugata facie' taken as 'with a wrinkled/frowning face'. In line 18, 'Ante certe malum odire debemus hominem' is awkward; taken as 'before all we ought to hate the evil man, i.e. his vice, not his nature'. In line 20 the quotation from 1 Pet. 5:9 is rendered as the text gives it.

Line 22: 'In pace in idipsum' (Ps 4:9) rendered literally as 'in the selfsame' to keep the link with the lemma 'idipsum'. Line 23: 'mora est' read as 'mors est' (Rom 8:6); 'Dei et diaboli' is as printed, though the following examples treat prudence of God (spirit) and of the flesh. Line 24: 'superbe manendo residere' read with the editor's correction 'resistere'; 'ex .Egypto' read as flight into Egypt. Line 25: 'sede superbos, hi erant' read as 'sede super eos, hi erunt' (Isa 47:14); 'virtus es' read as 'victus es'; the quotation 'Fructus autem spiritus est' breaks off in the text as given.

ab17-ab22: section headings kept as separate lines. 26: 'putum' read as 'potum' (drink); 'exhiheaDIUS' as 'exhibeamus'. 27 (opp-lat1.27): 'Uiliges' read as 'Diliges'; 'Mima' as 'anima'. 28: 'prodhum' read as 'proditum' (betrayed). 'qui diligit omnem legem' is awkward; rendered as whoever loves him loves the whole law. 'in dilectione Dei æqualitatem, in proximi vero dilectione quantitatem' looks garbled or inverted (equality would fit love of neighbour, 'as yourself'); translated as printed, with '[he set]' supplied. 29: 'qui Evangelium respuunt, sicut Manichæi' contradicts the sense (Manichaeans rejected the Old Testament); 'Evangelium' is probably an error for 'legem', rendered '[the law]'. 'Audiuntur inter vos fornicatores' differs from the usual 'auditur inter vos fornicatio'; translated as given. 'qui habet scientiam matrem virtutum' is obscure; translated literally.

Line 31 breaks off mid-word ('Dominu[s]'); the edition's following text is not in this stretch. The Ephesians reference printed as (III, 33) should be 3:13. In line 32 '(Cod., cor]' is an editorial note recording a manuscript variant and is left out. Scanning errors read as evident: 'omnia scriba' as omnis scriba; 'comprehendere .lent' as solent; 'stellas cren' as stellas caeli; 'harhQue' as namque. In line 32 the passage on angelic fatherhood is obscure; 'Dicuntur enim angeli minoris ordinis' is taken as 'those of the lesser order are called [simply] angels'. In line 34 the lemma's list omits 'longitudo' in the second citation, as in the text.

Several scanning errors read as evident (e.g. 'consnevit' = consuevit, 'Supcreminens', 'UNA FLUES' = una fides, 'ba p ismum'). Para. 35: 'ET AUTEM' read as 'EI AUTEM'. Para. 37: 'elevari' (raised up) is odd; perhaps for 'evelli' or 'avocari'. 'Beati mites, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt' conflates two beatitudes; translated as given. Para. 38: 'innuuntur' rendered 'are signed' (perhaps for 'imbuuntur', 'are imbued'); 'idem subjecit, alius autem sic...' cites 1 Cor 7:7, attributed loosely. Lemma in para. 39 reads 'unus Dominus et Pater' for 'unus Deus et Pater', as later in the paragraph.

Line 40: 'Patea' read as 'Pater'. Line 45: the sentence 'quilibet homo quam promptus esset ad bonum faciendum... saltim quasi mensura' is defective; the edition itself marks it as standing so in the codex, and the translation is tentative. 'spiritalibus paribus' read as 'spiritalibus panibus' (spiritual loaves); 'det Uti' read as 'det illis'.

In ref 48 the Latin 'pullus' (twice) is evidently a misreading of 'psalmus' and has been translated as such; likewise 'pullIs' in ref 47 is read as 'nullus'. In ref 48 the phrase 'omnia ista repleta impleri poterit' is flagged by the edition ('Ita Cod.') and its sense is uncertain. In ref 49 the Solomon quotation 'Principem te constituere' is read as 'Principem te constituerunt?' (Sirach 32:1). The phrase 'Deo scilicet Dei Filio ... et ideo Patri' is obscure in the Latin and has been rendered literally.

In ref. 51 'viva' is read as 'vitia' (vices). 'acreum' read as 'aereum' (airy); 'de annis' (ref. 53) read as 'de armis'; 'quidem virtutem' read as 'quandam virtutem'. In ref. 51 the sentence 'Spiritalia enim nequitiae fuit, qui habitat in coelestibus' is syntactically odd and may be corrupt; also the clause 'et omnes peccatores tenebrae aliquoties mutantur' seems to lack a connective. 'Est enim colluctatio adversus carnem et sanguinem' may originally have read 'Non est'. 'Deorsum fluens' is the traditional etymology of 'diabolus'.

Line 55: 'Quos enim caro semel copulaverit' ('whom the flesh has once joined') makes poor sense; probably a misreading of charitas, rendered 'charity'. 'ita et infirmiter tenendo' read as firmiter; 'malum intelligi vult' taken as magis; 'fruebit [Ita Cod.] illam' rendered as 'will enjoy it'. Line 56: 'Ore ut' read as Oro ut; 'sensus montis' as mentis. Line 57: 'Aptavi vos' rendered as the familiar 'despondi' ('I have espoused').

Line 1: 'apostolos' read as 'apostolus'. 'Orando est, qui stant ne cadam' is corrupt; translated as if 'orandum est ut qui stant ne cadant'. 'De quo [Ita Cod,]' introduces an incomplete sentence; the edition marks the manuscript reading as is. 'Confirmati a quo?' comments on a lemma (Vulgate 'confortati') not quoted in the text. Line 59: the edition notes the manuscript reads 'persecuti' for 'perfecti'. Line 60: 'mansuetudinem' (meekness) makes little sense beside 'dignitatem' and may be an error for 'magnitudinem' (greatness).

Line 61: 'Unum corpus' comments on a lemma ('in one body') not printed in the text. Line 62: 'quod [Cod., quem] nullus volet' translated as 'valet' (be able). 'decalogum doctrinae' rendered literally as 'tenfold teaching'; sense uncertain. Line 64: 'tradidit cum Judas' read as 'eum'; 'De....' read as 'Deus'; the Peter quotation is garbled in the edition and is translated as it stands.

Line 65: the codex reads 'volunt ea movere' (marked [Ita Cod.]); the sense and the Gospel require 'nolunt', so 'will [not]' is supplied. Line 66: 'bitumum' (so the codex) taken as bitumen. Line 67: 'bonorum Metrorum' read as 'bonorum vestrorum'; 'vincti compassi estis' rendered in the sense of the Vulgate 'vinctis'. Line 68: 'Iutae' read as 'Lucae' (Luke); 'prædilectionem' as 'per dilectionem'. Line 69: the derivation 'Phari Graece' is the author's (Latin fari, Greek φάναι); 'ostendit quoddam vaticinium fuisse ex Filio Dei' is obscure; 'per modos' in the list of ways is probably an error for 'per verba', as the following examples show.

Line 72 breaks off mid-sentence ('...sanguinis Christianum'); 'Christianum' is probably a misreading for 'Christi', and the sentence is incomplete in the text as held. Line 70: 'Utitur hoc apud haereticos' taken as 'he uses this against the heretics'. Line 71: 'numen de lumine' read as 'lumen de lumine'. Line 73: the opening 'Humiliatio enim ultima intelligitur' is obscure and possibly corrupt; 'Humiles non oportet esse' read as 'nos oportet' (the sense requires it). Line 74: 'Scilicet aut per dexteram' seems defective (a contrasting 'per sinistram' clause may be lost).

The lemma reads 'aeternam suam gratiam' ('his eternal grace'), whereas the commentary (and the Vulgate) has 'gloriam' ('glory'); translated as given. '[Cod., incoronari]' is the editor's report of the manuscript reading. Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Forit' for 'Foris', 'reddin- pti' for 'redempti', 'mul- Ii.' for 'multis', 'sit Dbminus' for 'ait Dominus').

nodes.text: AT THAT TIME. LUCULENTIUS.
COMMENTARIES OF LUCULENTIUS ON SOME PARTS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, FROM ANCIENT MANUSCRIPTS OF THE VATICAN AND VALLICELLIAN LIBRARIES.
I.
Reading of the holy Gospel according to Matthew (6:24): At that time Jesus said to his disciples: No one can serve two masters, and the rest.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

Some want to understand [the two masters as] Christ and the devil, between whom there can be no fellowship. For what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial, or what share has the believer with the unbeliever? [The answer] understood: none. But who the two masters are he next makes plain when he adds: YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON. For he did not say that those who have riches cannot serve the Lord, but those who serve riches. For many who have riches do not distribute them as masters, but guard them as slaves. Of such the Apostle says: He stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and of revelation in the judgements of God. And on the other side, many have riches and distribute them as masters, and do not guard them as slaves, like Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Job, and the others who knew how to govern their riches well by distributing them faithfully. FOR EITHER HE WILL HATE THE ONE AND LOVE THE OTHER, that is, God; OR HE WILL BEAR WITH THE ONE AND DESPISE THE OTHER. He did not say "hates", but "will despise"; therefore he does not fear [him]. For no one is so mad as to say that he hates God; but God hates the one who despises his commandments, as the prophet says: You have hated all who work iniquity. For just as sweet and bitter cannot both flow together from one spring, so no one can serve two masters alike, namely God and riches. You cannot serve God and mammon. Mammon is Syriac, and in Latin it is called riches. No one can serve God and riches alike, because one who serves God with his whole heart cannot be a slave of riches. Whatever a man loves more, that [is his god]: the greedy man has gold as his god, and of gluttons the belly is god. Their end is destruction; their god is the belly, and their glory is in the shame of those who mind earthly things. And what shall I say? Whatever a man loves more than God, that is certainly his god; and therefore no one can serve God and mammon, because one who devotes himself to greed cannot serve God: for where your treasure is, there is your heart also.

THEREFORE I SAY TO YOU, DO NOT BE ANXIOUS FOR YOUR SOUL, WHAT YOU SHALL EAT. Since food concerns the body more than the soul, why does he say: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat? But we ought to understand "soul" in this place as the present life, as also in many places of Scripture, such as that of David: These men put their souls in their hands; and: My soul is always in my hands. The apostle Paul too: Nor do I count my soul more precious than myself. So also here, when he says: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, it is as if he said: for your life, how you may be able to live. But it is asked why he says: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, when Paul says: Not slothful in diligence. But there a spiritual diligence is to be understood, in which we must not be slothful, because we ought to seek with eagerness the things that are of the Spirit. As for what concerns the outer man, labour indeed is to be practised, but anxiety removed. Of this the Lord said to the Jews, when he saw them toiling in earthly desire: Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures to eternal life. And therefore work is indeed to be practised, as the apostle Paul said: Whoever will not work, let him not eat. And elsewhere: Let them work in quietness and eat. And this is what he says: Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat; as if he said: He who has given the greater things will certainly grant the lesser also; for he who made the soul and the body will also give support. IS NOT THE SOUL MORE THAN FOOD? AND THE BODY MORE THAN CLOTHING? The soul is more than food, because it will remain for ever, but food will perish. And the body is more than clothing, because although it is reduced to ashes, it will nevertheless be re-formed in the likeness of the former. For it is written: Like a garment you will change them, and they will be changed; but clothing is reduced to nothing.

LOOK AT THE BIRDS OF THE AIR, FOR THEY DO NOT SOW, NOR GATHER INTO BARNS, AND YOUR HEAVENLY FATHER FEEDS THEM. He had given a comparison from the greater to the lesser, from the soul to the body, and from the lesser to the greater, from food to the soul; now again he gives a comparison from the lesser to the greater, from birds to man, when he says: Look at the birds of the air. Someone wanted to understand the birds of the air as angels, because of this: One of the seraphim, says the prophet, flew to me; [angels] who do not labour. For they indeed enjoy the vision of God, as the apostle Peter says: Into whom the angels long to look. But this must by no means be understood so, as if man were better before God than the angels. It is better that we understand the birds of the air as the birds that roam through this air, which is why they are called birds of the air: they do not labour nor reap, but feed with beak and claws. If, he says, God so feeds the birds of the air, whose soul dies with the body, how much more you, who are made in the image of God, [more] than them? For this reasoning is to be understood not by number but by comparison. If you understand it by number, the birds of the air are more than men; but what he says is to be understood by worth and comparison: ARE YOU NOT MUCH MORE THAN THEY? That is, you are both better and dearer, and worth more. For with them, if the soul is harmed, the body will perish; man dies in the body, [but] the soul goes towards heavenly things. For almighty God did not make men for the sake of birds, but birds for the sake of men; and he came into the world for the sake of men, not of birds, and bought them at a dear price, as it is written: For you were bought with a great price. AND WHICH OF YOU BY TAKING THOUGHT CAN ADD ONE CUBIT TO HIS STATURE? For no one can add one cubit to his stature; indeed, not even make one hair of his head white or black. A comparison had to be given of clothing to the body, as one had been given of the soul. What he says is of this kind: leave the care to him who made your stature; for he who set the body at whatever measure he willed, namely how long, how short it should be, will certainly give what is less, namely clothing and covering. For he who has bestowed the greater things will surely grant the lesser also.

CONSIDER THE LILIES OF THE FIELD, HOW THEY GROW: THEY DO NOT LABOUR, NOR DO THEY SPIN. In this place let us understand not the lily specifically, but all plants, which in winter seem withered, and in summer are adorned with various flowers. Let us understand the field as this world, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: For the field is the world. They do not labour at spinning, nor at weaving, nor at setting up the warp, but grow by the providence of God. BUT I SAY TO YOU THAT NOT EVEN SOLOMON IN ALL HIS GLORY WAS ARRAYED LIKE ONE OF THESE. Why is it that, passing over so many kings who were before Solomon or after him, he preferred him to all? Surely because of his wisdom or riches, since he was wiser or richer than all, as God said to him: Because you have not asked for yourself riches of gold and silver, nor many days, nor the lives of your enemies, but wisdom to discern good and evil, behold, I have given you wisdom to discern good and evil; behold, I have given you wisdom, so that you may be wise above all who were before you. Moreover, what you did not ask, I will give you also: the riches of the world, of gold and silver. Yet in all his abundance of riches and variety of clothing he was not arrayed like one of these, understood: the lilies of the field. For neither silk, nor the purple of kings, nor the embroidery of weavers can be compared with flowers. For what is as red as the rose? What is as white as the lily? As for the purple of the violet, that it is surpassed by no murex dye is a judgement for the eyes rather than for words. For Solomon made golden vessels in the house of the Lord, as befitted royal dignity. And Solomon also made a litter of the wood of Shittim; he made its pillars of silver, its ascent of purple, its couch of gold; the middle he spread with love for the daughters of Jerusalem. Now the litter signifies the holy Church, and the pillars the holy teachers, as was said of some of them: James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars. The purple ascent signifies the holy confessors, the golden couch divine wisdom, of which it is said elsewhere: A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise. The daughters of Jerusalem signify holy souls. For although Solomon had been so adorned, yet he could never have a garment as white as the lily, nor as purple as the violet, nor as scarlet as the rose. Spiritually, by the lily virginity is signified, by violets the confessors, by roses the martyrs. For Solomon did not have virginity; indeed his heart was even corrupted by women.

IF GOD SO CLOTHES THE GRASS OF THE FIELD, WHICH IS HERE TODAY AND TOMORROW IS THROWN INTO THE OVEN. Here it is plainly given to be understood that above he meant to include every kind of plant when he says: If the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven. He put 'today' for the present time, 'tomorrow' for the future; as in that [saying] of Jacob: TOMORROW MY RIGHTEOUSNESS WILL ANSWER FOR ME. And Samuel said to Saul: Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. HOW MUCH MORE YOU, O YOU OF LITTLE FAITH? The faith of the apostles is rebuked, or of the Jews, who have little faith. THEREFORE DO NOT BE ANXIOUS, SAYING: WHAT SHALL WE EAT, OR WHAT SHALL WE DRINK, OR WITH WHAT SHALL WE BE CLOTHED? Above he had removed anxiety about food and clothing; about drink he had kept silent. Summing up, he adds: Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed? Understood [is]: exquisite feasts; or what shall we drink: how many kinds of drinks; or with what shall we be clothed: namely, costly garments. ALL THESE THINGS THE GENTILES SEEK. These things which were said above, namely eating, drinking, putting on costly garments, all these and things like them the Gentiles sought, who were like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding, not knowing the Lord. FOR YOUR HEAVENLY FATHER KNOWS THAT YOU NEED ALL THESE THINGS. There were some who said: If God knows everything that is necessary for us, why do we need to ask him? For he knows all things. Yet he is to be asked and entreated. For he himself says: Ask and you will receive, seek and you will find. We ought also to live by the labours of our hands, because it was said to the first man: In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread. BUT SEEK FIRST THE KINGDOM OF GOD AND HIS RIGHTEOUSNESS, AND ALL THESE THINGS WILL BE ADDED TO YOU. The kingdom of God is taken in many ways, but here by the kingdom of God is understood either the Son of God or holy Scripture, both of which we ought to seek. The Son of God, as the prophet says: Seek the Lord and be strengthened, seek his face always. Or holy Scripture, by reading and searching which we can find how we may keep his righteousness and precepts, or how we may deserve to be rewarded by him. And all these things will be added to you; namely, the things said above will be added to you. He did not say 'will be given', but 'will be added'; for whatever we receive in the present is worthless in comparison with the rewards above; and therefore those things which are greater are to be sought first, namely the kingdom of God and his righteousness, so that these things which are necessary for the body may be added, and greater things given besides.
II.
Reading of the holy Gospel according to John (1:29): At that time John saw Jesus coming to him from Nazareth, and said to him: Behold the Lamb of God, etc.
HOMILY OF LUCULENTIUS.

Rightly does blessed John call Jesus, the Son of God, a lamb; for [he is] a lamb because innocent. This is the lamb of whom Isaiah had spoken long before: He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he will be dumb, and he did not open his mouth. Of this lamb John [says] in the Apocalypse: The lamb that was slain by you from the foundation of the world; for the lamb was slain in Abel, offered in Isaac, sacrificed in Egypt; for he himself, coming into the world, fulfilled in truth whatever had before been said or done concerning him in figures, when, as the world drew to its evening, he was sacrificed for us on the altar of the cross, as the Apostle says: For Christ our passover has been sacrificed. BEHOLD THE LAMB OF GOD. The particle 'behold' is an adverb of one pointing out: for because blessed John saw with his eye, he pointed with his finger; rightly did he say: Behold the Lamb of God. The apostles too were called lambs, as the Lord says: Behold, I send you as lambs among wolves. Well [called] lambs, because innocent, because simple; in the likeness of the true lamb, of whom we spoke above. John too was a lamb, because he too was innocent as far as Christ [was]. For we are all born with sin, as the prophet says: In iniquities I was conceived. He alone came without sin, he alone was free of the stain of sin. For he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, yet without sin. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. He took flesh from Adam; he did not take sin. And therefore, because he did not take sin from our lump, he is the one who takes away our sin. But someone says: What does that Lamb of God profit us? Behold the lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world. He took away the sin of the world, because, doing signs and miracles, he gave light to the blind and raised the dead. Moreover he said with power to whom he wished: Your sins are forgiven you. He also took away the sins of the world when, as he hung on the cross, from his opened side flowed blood and water. Hence Peter says of him: He bore our sins in his body on the tree. He takes away the sins of the world daily through the partaking of his body and blood. For they say that as fire consumes stubble, so [are] lesser sins [consumed] through the partaking of his body and blood. For he himself says: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you. And again: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.

But it may be asked why the Son of God wished to come to baptism, when he had no sin which he would have needed to expiate. Surely because there were to be in the Church catechumens of higher birth who would disdain to come to baptism, saying to themselves: Am I to receive what that man has? I am better than that one and that one of the faithful. To break their pride he deigned to come to the baptism of a servant, as if he were addressing the proud man and saying: Why do you exalt yourself? Why do you stretch yourself? How great in power is your grace? How great in excellence? Can you be greater than I? If I came to the baptism of a servant, how [can] you disdain to come to the baptism of the Lord? Or surely he wished to be baptized in order to give sanctification and purification to all waters. Or else to give an end to the Old Testament and begin the New. For he was under the law until, being baptized, he gave an end to the law of the Old Testament and a beginning to the grace of the holy Gospel. He wished to be baptized to teach all humility. Hence, as the other evangelists say, when he came to John to be baptized by him, John said to him: Do you come to me to be baptized? I ought to be baptized by you. And the Lord [said] to him: Let it be so now, that all righteousness may be fulfilled. What is 'that all righteousness may be fulfilled', except that all humility may be fulfilled? As if he said: I came to die; I did not come to be baptized. I have to die for men; I do not have to be baptized for men. And surely he who received his passion from wicked servants ought to receive baptism from a good servant. THIS IS HE OF WHOM I SAID: AFTER ME COMES A MAN WHO WAS MADE BEFORE ME. Where had John said this of the Lord? When, questioned by the priests and Levites, he denied that he was the Christ, Elijah, or the prophet. As they still inquired: Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet? he answered and said: I baptize in water, but among you has stood one whom you do not know. He repeats this very thing, saying: After me comes a man who was made before me. Rightly he calls him a man, for of him the prophet says: Behold a man, the Dayspring is his name. He comes after me who was born afterwards. For blessed John went before the Son of God in conception, in birth, in passion. Who was made before me, that is, was preferred to me, BECAUSE HE WAS BEFORE ME: he was before me because in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was with God, and God was the Word. Before John, before Mary too, for he himself made Mary, and he himself was born through Mary. Before every creature too, as he himself says in Wisdom: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything, from the beginning. And: Before the morning star I begot you. AND I DID NOT KNOW HIM; BUT THAT HE MIGHT BE MADE MANIFEST IN ISRAEL, FOR THIS REASON I CAME INTO THE WORLD BAPTIZING IN WATER. He says 'that he might be made manifest in Israel', that is, to the people of Israel itself. For this reason John was sent baptizing in water, to make the Son of God manifest to the people of Israel, because he was coming hidden, so that he could scarcely have been recognized by a few, or by none. Hence John himself says elsewhere: I baptize in water, but among you stands one whom you do not know. He baptized only with water; he could not forgive sins, just as priests in the Church now do. They dip bodies in water, but no one can forgive sins except God alone.

AND JOHN BORE WITNESS, BECAUSE I SAW THE SPIRIT DESCENDING. Another evangelist says that the Lord, after being baptized, at once came up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit descending like a dove, and it remained upon him. The heavens are opened when the Lord is baptized, and the Holy Spirit descends upon him, so that we might be given to understand that every human being, before he comes to baptism, has the entrance to the heavenly kingdom closed because of original sin; but in baptism the evil spirit goes out, and the Holy Spirit begins to dwell [in him], as the Apostle says: You know that you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you. In this place you have the whole Trinity contained. The Father is heard in the voice, the Son [is shown] in the name, the Holy Spirit is shown in the dove. But why is it that the Holy Spirit did not wish to be shown in the likeness of any other bird except the dove? Surely because the dove is a simple creature, and a stranger to the dregs of malice. [This was] to show that no one can receive the Holy Spirit unless he has been made simple. For some have wished to receive the Holy Spirit in the form of a raven, as was Simon Magus, who offered money to the holy apostles, saying: Give me this power, that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit. He wanted to buy what he would sell at a higher price, and therefore he heard from Peter: May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. You will have no part or lot in this word. So whoever desires to receive the Holy Spirit ought to seek him in the dove, that is, in simplicity. Because of what is written: In simplicity of heart seek him. And the Lord says to the disciples: Be wise as serpents, and simple as doves.

AND I DID NOT KNOW HIM. What does he mean when he says 'I did not know him', when he had already borne so many and such great testimonies? For he had already pointed him out with his finger, he had already said: Behold the Lamb of God. For if he did not know him, how did he say to him when he came to him to be baptized: You come to me? I ought to be baptized by you. But it must be understood that there was something in him that he did not know, and something that he knew. He knew the Lord, he knew the Son of God, but he did not yet know that the Lord would keep the power of baptizing for himself, and would transfer it to none of his servants. This he knew [not], and this he learned through the dove. For if he gave the power to anyone, perhaps some would choose for themselves holier men by whom to be baptized. But whether a good man or a bad man baptizes in ministry, in power [it is he]; for he it is who baptizes: whether an adulterer or a chaste man or a drunkard baptizes, he is the one who baptizes. Whether a dove or a kite baptizes, he is the one who baptizes. Let Peter baptize, let Paul baptize, let Judas baptize, he is the one who baptizes, who forgives sins, who bestows the Holy Spirit, who says to his disciples: John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit. This blessed John did not know about the Lord, and this he learned through the dove. BUT HE WHO SENT ME TO BAPTIZE IN WATER SAID TO ME: HE ON WHOM YOU SEE THE SPIRIT DESCENDING AND REMAINING UPON HIM, THIS IS HE WHO BAPTIZES IN THE HOLY SPIRIT AND FIRE. And John bore witness, saying: THAT THIS IS THE SON OF GOD. Blessed John saw the heavens opened above the Lord, he saw the Holy Spirit descending in a dove. He heard the voice of the Father saying: This is my beloved Son. And therefore he said: I SAW, AND I BORE WITNESS that this is the Son of God. But it should be noted that he says: He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him. For the Holy Spirit descended upon the baptized Lord in such a way that he would never depart from him. For he committed no sin for which [the Spirit] would have had to depart from him. But he would not say 'remaining upon him' unless [the Spirit] sometimes departed from the saints, either through evil thoughts or through evil deeds. For it is written: The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful. And again: For perverse thoughts separate from God; for there is no man on earth who does good and does not sin. As the apostle says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. And again: In many things we all offend. But upon the baptized Lord he came so that he would never depart from him. And therefore in the Son alone was the Father well pleased, as he says: You are my beloved Son, in you I am well pleased. And the prophet: The Lord swore to him, and he will not repent. But of mortals it is written that the Lord said: For I repent that I made man upon the earth.
III.

Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Romans (12:1): Brothers, I beseech you by the mercy of God to present [your] bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

The apostle Paul had said above how all observance of God's commandments had passed from the Jews to the gentiles. Now he exhorts all, namely the gentiles and those who had come to the faith from the circumcision, to keep unshaken the faith they had received; indeed, that just as they had formerly been accustomed [to offer] sacrifices of dead animals, so now they should begin to offer themselves as a living sacrifice to God, saying: I BESEECH YOU BY THE MERCY OF GOD. Between 'asking' and 'beseeching' there is this difference: we ask about the smallest things, we beseech for the greatest. But the Apostle besought the Romans, that is, asked them earnestly, saying: I beseech you by the mercy of God. As if he were saying: I beseech you by the mercy of him who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light, and I beseech you by that mercy by which you were reconciled to God, not through philosophy, nor through any worldly wisdom, not through power, not through persuasive words; but I beseech you by the mercy of God by which you were reborn in the font of baptism. What he beseeches them for he reveals when he adds: THAT YOU PRESENT YOUR BODIES AS A LIVING SACRIFICE. It was the custom of the children of Israel, and the law commanded it, that they should offer sacrifice to God: calves, rams and goats, lambs, turtledoves or pigeons, and the other things that were commanded in the law. But what they did carnally with beasts befits us specially in our bodies. For our bodies are both a sacrifice and living: a sacrifice, because the flesh is mortified; living, because the spirit is given life, according to the precept of the same apostle, who says: Mortify your members which are upon the earth. Or because in the good dwells he who says: I am the way, the truth and the life. And of whom the Apostle [says]: That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts. For the ancients offered to God dead sacrifices of beasts, but now we offer ourselves as a living sacrifice, when we mortify vices and sins in ourselves and nourish virtues, fulfilling what the same Apostle says: That each of you should know how to possess his vessel in sanctification and honour. We possess the vessel in sanctification and honour when we slaughter vices in ourselves and are made holy through good works, as the Lord says: Be holy, because I the Lord your God am holy. And the Psalmist: A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise. Many seem to live, but are dead. As Paul writes of the widow: The widow living in pleasures is dead. And the Psalmist of such people: Let them go down alive into hell. Such people do not offer themselves to God as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God. When he had said 'holy', he added 'pleasing to God', because many seem holy to men but are reprobate before God; of whom it is written: There are ways which seem right to men, whose end sinks down to the depth of hell. And therefore it is necessary that each person, in the good he does, should strive to please not men but God, lest it be said to him: You have received your reward. Whoever does this will be able to become a sacrifice pleasing to God.

YOUR REASONABLE SERVICE. This refers to what was said above, that they offered calves, rams and the like. What they did carnally, we [must do] now spiritually; what they did in figure, we must do in truth. For, as the Apostle says: All things happened to them in figure. And therefore the Apostle commands us to present a reasonable service, saying: Your reasonable service. The teachers say there is this distinction between 'rational' and 'reasonable': that 'rational' relates to reason and good works, while 'reasonable' relates to discernment. And he rightly says 'your reasonable service', because that former service of yours was not reasonable. For it is foolish that dead carcasses should be offered to the living and invisible God. For as a dead thing renders no service to a living one, so no one can worthily offer calves or rams to the immortal and incorporeal God. AND DO NOT BE CONFORMED TO THIS WORLD, BUT BE REFORMED IN THE NEWNESS OF YOUR MIND. 'The world' [here] is not the circuit of heaven and earth, which they call sun, moon, stars, trees, to which no one can conform himself; but the lovers of the world are so called. But the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness. To this world, that is, to the lovers of the world, no one ought to conform himself, because it is written: Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it. So whoever joins himself to a fool will share in his works. With the holy you will be holy; which he does who drives the works of the flesh from himself and works the fruits of the spirit. But whoever serves fornication, shamelessness and uncleanness conforms himself to this world, that is, to the lovers of the world. But we ought rather to be reformed, not outwardly but inwardly, as he says: In the newness of your mind, when, putting off the old man, we put on the new. Of which the same Apostle [says]: Though our outer man is corrupted, yet the one who is within is renewed from day to day. And elsewhere: Be renewed in the spirit of your mind. Then we are reformed in the newness of our mind, when we cleanse ourselves from all defilement of flesh and spirit. Whoever does this, it is said to him by God: You are all beautiful, my love, and there is no stain in [you].

THAT YOU MAY PROVE WHAT IS THE WILL OF GOD, GOOD AND WELL-PLEASING AND PERFECT. What the will of God is, no one can prove unless he has been reformed in mind and cleansed from the oldness of life. For just as a man tests food, whether it is salted or unsalted, sweet or bitter, hot or cold, so the will of God is proved by three qualities. For we are either approved or rejected in thought, speech and deed; because the will of God is good in thought, well-pleasing in speech, perfect in action. In many the will of God seems good, and well-pleasing and perfect, but it is not good: those who disfigure their faces, who do almsgiving, prayer and everything they do not for the Lord's sake but for the sake of men's favour. Which the Apostle did, who said: If I wished to please men, I would not be the servant of Christ. But in those the will of God is good, and well-pleasing and perfect, whatever they do. For just as, to give an example, a grain of wheat falling into the earth rises in the blade, is lifted up in the stalk, is sharpened in the ear, so is the will of God, as I said. The will of God is good in thought, well-pleasing in speech, perfect in action. Hence it is written: For with the heart one believes unto justice, with the mouth one confesses unto salvation. Otherwise: the will of God is good in the married, well-pleasing in the continent, perfect in virgins; or good in hope, fully good in faith, perfect in charity. And therefore the apostle Paul admonishes that in every act of ours, whether of thinking, or speaking, or doing anything, we should always seek with our whole intention what is pleasing to God.

FOR I SAY, THROUGH THE GRACE THAT HAS BEEN GIVEN TO ME, TO ALL WHO ARE AMONG YOU, NOT TO BE WISE BEYOND WHAT ONE OUGHT TO BE WISE. As is his custom, the Apostle speaks through the grace given to him, not in the persuasive words of human wisdom, not through philosophy or empty boasting, but he speaks through the grace given to him. For there is much difference between one who speaks through grace and one who speaks through human boasting. For many speak rhetorically in brilliant and well-composed language, but do not edify their hearers; for they can stir no one to compunction, because what they say in words they destroy by deeds. Such people do not speak through the grace which was given to Paul. And on the other side there are others who speak not with great eloquence, but only simply and without artifice, yet they have converted their hearers and many of the unbelievers, rather by doing good. And this is to speak through the grace which was given to Paul. To all who are among you, that is, to priests, deacons, and all who are in the church. But what does he mean by saying, not to be wise beyond what one ought to be wise? Since no one can know all things fully, because eye has not seen, nor ear heard, how great and what kind of things God has prepared for those who love him. And again: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgements, and unsearchable his ways! For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. And here he says: all schismatics, all the proud, who think wrongly of God; all who teach what neither the Lord nor the apostles taught—all these are wise beyond what one ought to be wise. It can [also be understood] against the proud Romans, who exalted themselves against the olive, to whom the same [Apostle] says: Do not boast against the branches; but if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you. You say then: The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in. But they were broken off because of unbelief. But you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. BUT TO BE WISE UNTO SOBRIETY. Sobriety, as is handed down by our forebears, is one of the four principal virtues, which are prudence, fortitude, temperance and justice. Temperance itself is also sobriety, which must be kept not only outwardly, on account of this: Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness, but inwardly. Therefore to be wise unto sobriety [is] to be wise with temperance. Hence the same [Apostle] also says: Not minding high things, but consenting to the humble. And another Scripture: Do not seek things higher than you, and do not search out things stronger than you,

AND TO EACH AS GOD HAS ALLOTTED THE MEASURE OF FAITH. It is understood: so let him be wise. And he rightly says, the measure of faith, because as much faith as anyone has, so great a gift he receives. [To one is given] through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, according to the same Spirit, dividing to each as he wills. And again: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit, that is, according to his own capacity, as much as human frailty can receive. Similar to this is: Having gifts differing according to the grace which has been given to you. FOR AS IN ONE BODY WE HAVE MANY MEMBERS, BUT ALL THE MEMBERS DO NOT HAVE THE SAME FUNCTION, SO WE, BEING MANY, ARE ONE BODY IN CHRIST. The apostle Paul speaks as a natural philosopher, discussing the members of men. For who can doubt that there are many members in the body, but they do not have one function? For the hand does not speak, nor does the mouth work, nor do the nostrils hear, nor do the ears smell; but the eyes see, the ears hear, the mouth speaks, the nostrils smell, the hands work, the feet run about; yet there is one body, and all the members need one another. For the hands cannot say to the ears: You are not necessary to me; nor the ears to the hands: We do not need your works. But if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it, as the Apostle says: You are the body of Christ, and members of your members. But not all the members have the same function, because one in the Church is an eye by seeing; another a mouth, who preaches rightly; another a hand by doing good; yet one cannot say to another: I do not need you, because we all need one another; just as any preacher cannot say to those under him: I do not need you, because he must receive provisions so that he may be able to fulfil the office entrusted to him. For the apostle Paul says: If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things? AND EACH ONE MEMBERS ONE OF ANOTHER, that is, I am an eye to you, he is a foot to me, you are a hand to me: thus we bear our burdens for one another, we are one body, and members one of another, fulfilling this: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. And this in Christ Jesus, because in him and through him all forbearance is given to us, and love, so that we may be able to bear with one another.
IV.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Romans (12:6): Brothers, having gifts differing according to the grace which has been given to you.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

A gift depends not on our choice but on the giver's. But the gifts which are given, which the Apostle enumerates in what follows, refer to the earlier passage where he had said: In one body we have many members; and they are rightly called gifts, because they are given from above: For every best given thing and every perfect gift is from above. And that saying of Paul: For what do you have that you have not received, and if you have received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? And he rightly says: DIFFERING ACCORDING TO THE GRACE WHICH HAS BEEN GIVEN TO YOU; because as much as the grace of the Holy Spirit bestows, so much does one receive, as he had said above: To each as God has allotted the measure of faith. For not just anyone receives this or that which he wants, but [what] the grace of the Holy Spirit deigns to bestow on him. And well [does he say] differing, because one gift differs from another. For I have what another does not have, and you have what I lack, and that other has what neither I nor you have. Thus one gift differs from another. To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge. No one has all things except him alone on whom the sevenfold Spirit rested, to whom God does not give the Spirit by measure. But the faithful among them all have all things.

OR PROPHECY ACCORDING TO THE PROPORTION OF FAITH. Now he begins to enumerate what the gifts are, putting prophecy in the first place. That is called prophecy which is not seen in the present but reaches forward into the future. And he said well, according to the proportion of faith, because faith merited it. For the law or prophecy is given according to faith, because as much faith as anyone has, so much he receives from the Lord, as Christ says: As you have believed, be it done to you. And: If you had faith as a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain: Be taken up and cast into the sea, and it would obey you. And in the Old Testament we read that some pleased God through faith; such as Abraham, of whom it is written: Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for justice. But more so in the New. OR MINISTRY, IN MINISTERING. He speaks of the ministers of the Church, namely deacons, subdeacons and the other orders, which whoever receives ought to exercise faithfully and carefully, on account of this: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom his lord has set over his household? And if anyone ministers, [let it be] as from the strength which God supplies. OR HE WHO TEACHES, IN TEACHING. He speaks of the teachers of the Church, who as faithful servants have received the ministry of preaching and do not hide what they have received. For it is written: Hidden wisdom and unseen treasure, what profit is there in either? And Daniel says: The learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto justice, like the stars for everlasting eternities. HE WHO EXHORTS, IN EXHORTING. Between teaching and exhorting there is this difference: he who teaches is greater than he who exhorts; one cannot teach unless he is taught, because he who has not been a disciple of truth will be a master of error. But we can all exhort, God granting it, [each one] who does good and urges others to carry it out. Hence the Apostle says to Titus: Speak these things and exhort. And the Lord in the Gospel: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

HE WHO GIVES, IN SIMPLICITY. He speaks of almsgivers, who supply the needy with what they need. On account of this [saying]: When you see a naked man, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh. Whoever does this ought to do it with simplicity, not with a frowning face. For God loves a cheerful giver; and if he loves a cheerful one, without doubt he hates a gloomy one. And elsewhere: In every gift make your face cheerful. Or he does it with simplicity so that praise is not sought from men. And on account of this: When you give alms, let your left hand not know. HE WHO PRESIDES, IN SOLICITUDE. He speaks of those who preside in the Church, who receive the place of teaching; he admonishes them to be solicitous over the flock entrusted to them, lest anyone perish through their sloth, and it be said to them: I will require his blood at your hand. These the same [Apostle] admonishes, saying: Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock. And again: Feed the flock of God which is among you. HE WHO SHOWS MERCY ought to do it IN CHEERFULNESS, according to the reasoning given above. Or he who instructs one ignorant of letters ought to do it with cheerfulness, as has been said: In every gift make your face cheerful. LOVE WITHOUT PRETENCE. To pretend belongs to the reprobate, who fear being punished; to love belongs to sons, and therefore there ought to be no pretence in a Christian. Many seem to love outwardly, [but] inwardly they contrive evil: Joab bore their type, who, holding Amasa's chin with his hand, drove a sword into his belly. Of such it is written: The pretender deceives his friend with his mouth. And the Psalmist: They have spoken vain things, each to his neighbour. And again: Who speak peace with their neighbour, but evils are in their hearts. But Christian men ought to be, as I have said, of love not feigned, but [shown] with the evidence of deeds, on account of this: Whoever sees his brother suffering need and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him?

HATING EVIL, CLINGING TO GOOD. Hating the evil one, that is the devil, of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: An evil man sowed tares over [the field] in the midst of the wheat, and went away; and the evil one came and snatched away. Clinging to the good, that is to Christ, saying with the Psalmist: But for me it is good to cling to God. Otherwise: he hates evil, that is vices and sins. Clinging to good, [that is] to the spiritual virtues which Paul enumerates, saying: The fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, and the rest like these. For it is not enough to hate evil unless one clings, conversely, to good. Of which the Psalmist says: Turn from evil and do good. Before all, certainly, we ought to hate the evil man, that is not his nature, but his vice. As he did who said: I have hated the wicked. Clinging to good, on account of this: With the holy you will be holy. LOVING ONE ANOTHER WITH BROTHERLY LOVE. For there is true brotherhood where there is true love, and therefore we ought to love one another, as the Lord says: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. For it should be known that brothers from the same womb love each other so much that one will give himself up to death for the other. And if they love each other so much, how much more ought spiritual [brothers] to love each other! For all of us redeemed in Christ are brothers, as the Lord says: For you are all brothers. Of which brotherhood holy David says: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell in unity! OUTDOING ONE ANOTHER IN HONOUR, that is, going before. For we all ought to love one another and go before [one another] in honour, on account of this: When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the nearest place. The same [Apostle] also says elsewhere: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. For you ought not to wait for someone to love you first, but rather you ought to go before him in loving, because if another loves you first, you no longer have so great a reward. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not the heathen do this?

NOT SLOTHFUL IN SOLICITUDE. Above he had said: He who presides, in solicitude; and here: Not slothful in solicitude. Above he had admonished [those who preside]; here he exhorts all. But what is it that he says: Not slothful in solicitude, when the Lord says: Do not be solicitous? And he himself elsewhere: Be solicitous about nothing. For in the things that are God's, which are necessary for the soul, we ought not to be slothful, [we ought] not to be [over-]anxious, that is, in fasts, in vigils, and prayer, and the like. But about transitory and perishable things we ought not to be solicitous. FERVENT IN SPIRIT; that is, warm, on account of this: Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out of my mouth. For with the lukewarm the Lord is nauseated, from the cold he suffers injury, in the fervent he dwells. Judas, because he was lukewarm, God vomited out. For just as flies do not come near a heated pot, but settle on a lukewarm one, so those who are fervent in that fire of which the Lord says: I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it be kindled? — evil spirits do not dare approach them, but they make sport of the lukewarm. And therefore in good work we ought to be not lukewarm but fervent. SERVING THE LORD, that is, obeying his precepts. REJOICING IN HOPE. He rejoices in hope who does not look at the things he sees, but awaits future joy. For hope that is seen is not hope, but [that] which is not seen. For in all that we suffer we ought to rejoice on account of hope, as the apostle James admonishes: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations. Rejoicing in hope, PATIENT IN TRIBULATION. For out of the joy of hope one endures tribulations, namely [knowing] that the rewards promised for them are much greater. And therefore we ought to rejoice in all tribulations, on account of this: Blessed are those who suffer persecution for justice's sake. And again: If you suffer anything for justice's sake, [you are] blessed.

INSTANT IN PRAYER. Prayer is very necessary, because, so that tribulation can be endured, one must persist in prayers. For constant prayer provides you help in adversity. And therefore he commands [us] to persist in prayer. And the Lord in the Gospel: Pray that your flight be not in winter or on the sabbath. And Peter: Watch therefore, praying at all times. SHARING IN THE NEEDS OF THE SAINTS. This can be understood in two ways: namely, that as the saints are afflicted, so we should be afflicted with them, on account of this: If we have been sharers in the sufferings, we shall also be [sharers] of the resurrection. And this: Knowing that the same suffering is happening to the true brotherhood which is in the world. Or else, [when they were] coming to the faith, the unbelievers plundered their substance; these the same Apostle praises: For you also suffered with those in chains, and accepted the plundering of your goods with joy. The Apostle exhorted the others: Remember the brothers who were in Jerusalem. As then, so also now, one must share in the needs of the saints; that is, in food and drink and clothing, and in all that a brother needs. For whoever has the substance of the world and sees his brother suffering need and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him? PURSUING HOSPITALITY. Hospitality is a great virtue. Through it certain men pleased God, having received angels as guests: like Abraham or Lot, who because of hospitality deserved to be delivered from Sodom. For we read that he not only received those who came, but drew [them in]; whence he also deserved to receive angels as his guests. Here it is given to be understood that guests are not only to be invited but even drawn in. Between receiving a guest and pursuing hospitality there is a great distance. Many receive guests who come to them, but this is not pursuing hospitality. But those who go round the villages and streets drawing guests, [even] unwilling, to their house — these are the pursuers of hospitality. For we have it written that two disciples of the Lord, compelling him to lodge [with them], deserved to recognise him in the breaking of bread, whom they had not recognised through the whole length of the journey. For it is written: Not the hearers of the law are just before God, but the doers of the law will be justified. Hence the Lord will say at the end: I was a stranger, and you took me in.

BLESS THOSE WHO PERSECUTE YOU, BLESS AND DO NOT CURSE. This is the very thing the Lord also says: Pray for those who persecute and slander you. For he himself did this first, when on the cross he asked the Father for those crucifying him, saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do. So we too ought to return good rather than evil to our enemies, on account of what Peter admonishes: Not returning evil for evil, nor curse for curse, but on the contrary blessing. There are many who do not curse, but bless in return. These fulfil the precept of the apostle Paul: TO REJOICE WITH THOSE WHO REJOICE, TO WEEP WITH THOSE WHO WEEP. Clearly it must be asked with whom one should rejoice and with whom one should weep. One should not rejoice with those who rejoice in acquiring temporal things, in abundance of gold and silver, and in the beauty of women, in the begetting of sons, who are glad when they have done evil and exult in the worst things. With such as these one should not rejoice, because of them it is written: Woe to you who laugh now! for you will mourn and weep. But one should rejoice with those who rejoice for the hope of eternal life, to whom the Lord says: Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven. Or with those who, placed in persecutions, rejoice, keeping the precept of the apostle James, who says: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations. To such the Lord says: I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice. Likewise one should weep not with those who grieve over the loss of things, over the death of parents, but we ought to weep with those who deplore their own sins, converted to the faith, lamenting what they have wickedly done, as he did who said: For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. With such as these one must weep, because it is written: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of joy, of an exultant banquet.

BEING OF ONE MIND TOWARD ONE ANOTHER. This saying seems on the surface more obscure than the others; yet we ought to be of one mind toward one another in what may not be varied: namely, what you hold of the Father, [hold] this of the Son, this of the Holy Spirit. As you have in the psalm: In peace in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest. What he says, 'the selfsame', can be understood otherwise: namely, that we should be of one accord with one will, as [is said] of the primitive Church in the Acts of the Apostles: They had one heart and one soul. That with one accord, with one mouth, you may glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Or certainly it can be understood of tribulations, in suffering with others, as above: To rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep: if one member suffers anything, all the members suffer with it; and if we have been sharers of the suffering, we shall also be [sharers] of the consolation. NOT MINDING HIGH THINGS, BUT REGARDING LOWLY THINGS. Because God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. And elsewhere it is written: For the root of all evils is pride. And the Psalmist: He knows high things from afar, that is, pride. And therefore, according to the precept of the apostle Peter, we ought to humble ourselves in the sight of God. For the Lord says thus: On whom shall I rest, but on the humble and quiet, and him who trembles at my words? And: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. Pride made demons out of angels, but humility [makes] angels out of men.
V.
Reading of the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Romans (12:16): Brothers, do not be wise in your own eyes.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

In the preceding chapter he had said: Not minding high things, that is, proud things. He adds: DO NOT BE WISE IN YOUR OWN EYES. We know of two kinds of prudence, of God and of the devil, of the flesh and of the spirit. Of the prudence of God the same one himself says: Be prudent as serpents. Of the prudence of the flesh the same apostle says: The prudence of the flesh is death; and: Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own sight! And it should be noted that he did not say only, Do not be prudent, but with the whole addition, in your own eyes. Prudent in his own eyes is he who wishes to avenge himself on his enemy, who curses back one who curses him, strikes back one who strikes him. Such a man is prudent in his own eyes. We ought to hold the prudence of the soul, so that we may be able to resist evil; by no means the prudence of the flesh, so as to avenge ourselves. RENDERING TO NO ONE EVIL FOR EVIL. None of us ought to render evil for evil, but rather good for evil, on account of this: Pray for those who persecute and slander you. He who renders evil for evil is a son of Adam; he who [renders] good for good is a son of man; he who [renders] evil for good is a son of the devil: like the Jews, to whom the Lord showed many good works, for which they killed him. And therefore they were called sons of the devil, the Lord saying to them: You are of [your] father the devil. But he who has rendered good for evil is a son of God, who prayed for the Jews crucifying [him], saying: Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do. PROVIDING GOOD THINGS NOT ONLY BEFORE GOD, BUT ALSO BEFORE ALL MEN. That is, doing good things, showing good, working good, not so that you may chase praise from men, on account of this: Take heed not to do your justice before men, to be seen by them; but for the sake of the goal of eternal life, or so that we may show a good example to others, the Lord saying: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven. And that [saying] of the Apostle: Having your conduct good among the gentiles, so that in that wherein they disparage you as evildoers, considering you from your good works, they may glorify the Lord in the day of visitation. He says 'all men': to Jews, Barbarians and Scythians, Greeks, Latins, and absolutely all we ought to show a good example; before God, that we may please him; before men, that they may imitate us.

IF IT CAN BE, AS FAR AS IT LIES WITH YOU, HAVING PEACE WITH ALL MEN. As far as it lies in us, we ought to have peace with all men, and say with the Psalmist: With those who hated peace I was peaceable. But human frailty is accustomed to say this: How can I have peace with one who persecutes me, who takes my goods from me? Hear the same apostle saying: Love of neighbour works no evil. But if some pagan, some schismatic, some heretic wishes to turn [us] aside from the way of truth, we neither can nor ought to have peace with them. But it is better to allow scandal to arise than that the truth of Christ be abandoned. Still, in them we ought to love the creature [and] hate the vice. NOT DEFENDING YOURSELVES, DEAREST ONES, that is, avenging [yourselves]. For none of us ought to defend himself, on account of this: If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. And: Pray for those who persecute and slander you. For in two ways we ought to GIVE PLACE TO WRATH, namely either by not resisting, or certainly by fleeing. We ought to give place to wrath by not resisting, not cursing back, not fighting back, not struggling against, according to the testimony cited above. We ought to give place to wrath by fleeing, as the Lord himself also did, who chose to turn aside by fleeing into Egypt. And elsewhere, when they wished to stone him, he hid himself from them, when, as the Gospel says, they took up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple. And of him it is written that Jesus began to do and to teach. For it is better to give place by fleeing than to resist by proudly staying. VENGEANCE IS MINE, I WILL REPAY, SAYS THE LORD. Thus the Lord says that he will avenge the injury of the saints as his own. And therefore none of us ought to avenge himself, because we have God as avenger, who will avenge our injuries as his own; who says through the prophet: He who touches you is as one who touches the pupil of my eye. And in the Gospel: Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it is fitting that a millstone be hung about his neck, and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea. Therefore vengeance is to be reserved to him who knows how to avenge the injuries of the saints in this way.

BUT IF YOUR ENEMY IS HUNGRY, FEED HIM. It is not enough for anyone not to render evil for evil unless, on the contrary, he gives or bestows the things [the other] needs; on account of this: He who has the goods of the world, and sees his brother in need, and shuts up his heart from him, how does the love of God abide in him? And especially with the word of preaching each one ought to feed his neighbour as far as he is able. FOR IN DOING THIS, YOU WILL HEAP COALS OF FIRE UPON HIS HEAD. There are some who feed their enemies with this intent, that they may heap coals of fire, that is, punishments, upon them. For he who feeds or gives drink to his enemy in such a way does not love him as himself. But we ought not to feed or give drink to our enemy in such a way, but rather so that we may turn him toward us, so that he who before held us hateful may begin to love [us]. He who loves his enemy in this way will heap coals of fire upon his head, that is, the love of charity. For dead coals, if they are joined to a live one, are usually kindled. So too he who before held us hateful, if he sees himself loved by us, himself begins to love us too. For it is written: With the holy you will be holy. These are the coals of which the prophet says: You have coals of fire, sit upon them, these will be a help to you. And we ought to understand that head of which the Lord [speaks] in the Gospel: Lift up your heads, for your redemption will draw near. DO NOT BE OVERCOME BY EVIL, BUT OVERCOME EVIL WITH GOOD. Do not be overcome by evil, that is, by him who persecutes and hates you: if he has made you like himself, you have been overcome by him. But overcome evil with good, that is, overcome his malice with patience. Otherwise: Do not be overcome by evil, that is, by the devil, of whom it is written in the Gospel that an evil man sowed tares over [it] in the midst of the wheat and went away. And this: Or make the tree bad and its fruits bad; by which is understood the devil and his evil works. But the good is Christ: whence it is said: Or make the tree good and its fruits good. Of whom [it is said] in the psalm: But for me it is good to cleave to God. In good overcome evil, in Christ the devil. Or certainly: do not be overcome by evil, that is, by sin, by the work of the flesh. But overcome evil with good, that is, with the fruit of the spirit, of which the same apostle says: But the fruit of the spirit is. Overcome evil, that is, sin, by putting to death the works of the flesh.
VI.
Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Romans (13:8): Brothers, owe no one anything, except to love one another.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

Above, the Apostle had admonished the Romans to pay their debt to all, saying: Render to all [their] due: to whom tribute, tribute; to whom honour, honour; to whom fear, fear; to whom toll, toll. Now he adds and says: OWE NO ONE ANYTHING, EXCEPT TO LOVE ONE ANOTHER. The Lord too commands us to do this very thing when he says: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's. For there is a debt which we ought to pay in this way: that is, if someone has harmed us or done us injury, [we ought] to pay this debt so that we do not answer evil for it any further, so that we may dare to say freely in the Lord's Prayer: Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. This that servant refused to do, to whom ten thousand talents were forgiven by his lord, and he himself refused to forgive his fellow servant a hundred denarii. There is another debt, namely sin, which we ought to pay in such a way that we do not return to it any further. Of which the same apostle says in another place: We are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. And there is a debt which we ought to pay in such a way that we always hold it; to hold it in such a way that we always pay it: namely charity, which we ought always to pay and always to hold. This is what he says: owe no one anything, except to love one another. For we ought never to cease from love of neighbour, namely that we provide food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold, and the other things we see them to be in need of, and always love God with the whole heart, and our neighbour as ourselves. And [we ought to do] this unfailingly, on account of this: He who perseveres to the end, he will be saved. Hence the same apostle says: Bear one another's burdens. And the Lord himself: A new commandment I give you, that you love one another. FOR HE WHO LOVES HIS NEIGHBOUR HAS FULFILLED THE LAW.

Love holds the first place both in the Old Testament and in the New. In the Old we have it written: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and your neighbour as yourself. In the New the Lord sums it up, when to the lawyer asking what was the greatest and first commandment of all, the Lord said: You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with your whole mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. And the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself. By 'neighbour' in this place we ought to understand not only a blood relative, but every man. If you choose to understand 'neighbour' only as a blood relative or kinsman, you seem to be given licence to pursue others with hatred, while keeping charity with your own alone. But it is better that you understand 'neighbour' as every man: whoever loves him as himself fulfils the law of Christ, who says: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. And this commandment we have from God, that he who loves the Lord should love his brother also. FOR: YOU SHALL NOT COMMIT ADULTERY. He who loves his neighbour as himself, that is, every man, cannot commit adultery with [his neighbour's] wife, because he himself does not want another to commit adultery with his wife, especially since the Apostle says: Fornicators and adulterers God will judge. And: Flee fornication, for every sin whatever that a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. YOU SHALL NOT KILL. And it is very plain that no one can kill his neighbour if he loves him as himself, because he himself does not want to be killed by anyone, knowing it is written: Everyone who kills with the sword shall perish by the sword, whether of God or of man. YOU SHALL NOT STEAL. And as we said above, no one steals from his brother if he loves him as himself, knowing it is written that thieves go to punishment. YOU SHALL NOT BEAR FALSE WITNESS: it is to be understood likewise, that he who loves his brother as himself cannot bring false testimony against him, on account of what is written: A false witness shall not go unpunished. Just as those two elders were not [unpunished] who bore false testimony against Susanna. And in the passion of the Lord and in that of blessed Stephen we read that false witnesses were present, none of whom could go unpunished.

YOU SHALL NOT COVET YOUR NEIGHBOUR'S PROPERTY. As we said above, so it is to be understood. But there is another neighbour, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, who, though he was our God, deigned to become our neighbour, as he himself says in the parable of the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. For when he had said that the priest and the Levite, having seen the wounded man, passed by and did not have pity, [but] a Samaritan passing by had pity, he at once added: Which of these three seems to you to have been neighbour to him who fell among robbers? And he said: He who showed mercy to him. He calls this one 'neighbour'; whoever loves him [loves] the whole law, and fulfils all the commandments in love of him. Of whom it is written: Christ is the end of the law. Nor can it in any way happen that someone who loves Christ with his whole heart and all his inmost being does anything that does not please Christ. For he does not adulterate his word if he truly loves him; just as the apostle did not do, who said: We are not adulterating the word of God, but as from God, before God, in Christ we speak. And the prophet in the psalm: You have destroyed all who go fornicating away from you. Such a man not only does not commit adultery, but does not even look at a woman to lust after her, but rather says with the Psalmist: My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? And not only does he not kill, but he is not even angry, on account of this: Everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment. Nor does he steal his words, as those did of whom he says: All who came before me were thieves and robbers. Nor does he bear false witness, knowing that the very one whom he loves was betrayed by false witness. Or [rather] he does not make him less than the Father, as the Arians do, who say the Father is greater, the Son less, and the Holy Spirit much less, speakers of falsehood and seducers [that they are]. AND IF THERE IS ANY OTHER COMMANDMENT, IT IS RENEWED IN THIS WORD. There are indeed other commandments, either those spoken of above or those carved on the tablets of stone, but they are renewed in this word, namely in the love of God and of neighbour, the Lord saying: On these two commandments hangs the whole law and the prophets. YOU SHALL LOVE YOUR NEIGHBOUR AS YOURSELF. And note that in the love of God [he set] equality, but in the love of neighbour quantity, when he said: as yourself. But the love of God is restricted by no measure. LOVE OF NEIGHBOUR WORKS NO EVIL. It is true, because he never works evil against his neighbour, since he loves him as himself. Or: he who loves Christ as himself works no evil, that is, does not commit sin, because everyone who is born of God does not sin. Love, therefore, is the fullness of the law, because all the commandments proceed from charity and reach all the way to it; without it virtues are reckoned vices. And this is what the Lord says through the prophet: The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth. For what can be shorter than that all things be concluded in two precepts? For if you are not able to search out everything, hold to these two, and you have fulfilled everything, whatever is open and whatever is hidden in the divine Scriptures.
VII.
Reading from the First Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Corinthians (1:4): Brothers, I give thanks to my God always for you, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

The Corinthians are Achaeans: these, having been preached to by Paul the apostle, after his departure abandoned his teaching and were led astray by false prophets. Wishing to reform this, the Apostle writes them two epistles. In the first he praises them at the beginning, [and] further on rebukes them sharply, in the manner of a skilled physician: for thus a skilled [physician] first touches the healthy flesh so as to reach the putrid; for if he touched the sick parts first, perhaps the patient would reject his medicine. So the Apostle first touched what was healthy in the Corinthians, when he began with praise: BROTHERS, I GIVE THANKS TO MY GOD ALWAYS FOR YOU FOR THE GRACE OF GOD WHICH HAS BEEN GIVEN YOU IN CHRIST JESUS. He came to the putrid parts when he said: Fornicators are heard of among you. For if they were rebuked in the first chapter, perhaps they would not accept his teaching. He says therefore: I give thanks to my God always for you. As if he were saying: I do indeed give thanks to God, who holds knowledge, the mother of the virtues; but I want you to know what that true knowledge is, where conduct agrees with life; not that which puffs up, but that which builds up. For knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. THAT IN ALL THINGS YOU HAVE BEEN MADE RICH IN HIM, IN ALL WORD AND IN ALL KNOWLEDGE. He shows that they were enriched in every good, since they came to the faith of Christ; namely in all virtues, in all word and in all knowledge, in both Testaments, Old and New. By 'in all word' he means in the law; by 'in knowledge', in the Gospel. For he is rich in all word and in all knowledge who is able to learn almost all the Scriptures and to instruct others. He is truly wise in all word and in all knowledge who preaches to others what he reads and understands, if he first fulfils it in deed, lest while preaching to others he himself become reprobate. Some are rich in all word, but not in all knowledge, as the Jews suppose [themselves], who keep only the letter of the law but reject the Gospel. There are others rich in knowledge, but not in word, who reject [the law], like the Manichaeans. By 'in all word' he means on the surface; by 'in knowledge', in spiritual understanding. And perhaps he says this because there were among the Corinthians those who were unwilling to accept both Testaments.
