And therefore, like a teacher, he spurs imperfect disciples on to better things by praising [them]. For so he says also to the Galatians: You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness.

EVEN AS THE TESTIMONY OF CHRIST WAS CONFIRMED IN YOU, SO THAT YOU LACK NOTHING IN ANY GRACE. By the testimony of Christ he means both Testaments, which either prophesied or showed the coming of Christ. Hence the Lord himself also [says]: Therefore every scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old. It was confirmed, he says, in you, that is, through my preaching; for [he taught] neither the New without the Old nor the Old without the New, but he taught them both, as he says elsewhere: For I delivered to you first of all what I also received; so that you lack nothing in any grace. Like this is what Solomon says: All good things came to me together with her. AS YOU AWAIT THE REVELATION OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. For him who is rich in all word and in all knowledge nothing remains but to await the revelation of the Lord, as the Lord says: Be ready, like men awaiting their lord when he returns from the wedding. This can be understood in two ways, both particularly and generally. Particularly, when the soul of each perfect man, departing from the body, passes to the Lord, as he himself says: I will, Father, that where I am, there my servant also may be. Generally, on the day of judgement, when we shall all stand before the tribunal of God. Hence also elsewhere: Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes. For each of the faithful ought so to live that he can await the revelation of the Lord, that is, that he may desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, because of what the Lord says: Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching.

WHO HAS CONFIRMED YOU TO THE END WITHOUT CRIME. For the saints await the revelation of the Lord, because now our life is hidden with Christ in God. But it will be revealed, because when Christ your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory. For now we are sons of God, and it does not yet appear what we shall be. But what we await will be revealed, because when he appears we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is. Who has also confirmed: who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. For he gave light to those who were in darkness and in the shadow of death. And this is what he says: who has also confirmed you. To the end, he says, that is, to death, or to the day of judgement. And note that he does not say without sin, but without crime. Nor does he seem contrary to John, who says: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Sin is one thing, crime another. By God's gift a man can be without crime, that is, without sacrilege, without adultery, without theft, or a greater crime; but without sin, no one. For there is no man on earth who does good and does not sin. For in many things we all offend. And therefore he does not say without sin, but without crime. ON THE DAY OF THE COMING OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, or on the day of death, when he deigns to come to his own. Hence also he says: So I will him to remain until I come. Or on the day of judgement, when he is to come to judge the living and the dead. Rightly is it said, on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence also Matthew: When the king sits on the throne of his kingdom and begins to judge. That day will be bitter to the unjust, gentle and mild to the just and the devout, to whom the Lord will say: Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you from the origin of the world. But to the reprobate: Go, accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for you. Foreseeing this day the prophet says: That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of mist and whirlwind, a day of cloud and trumpet blast. Of which another prophet also [says]: Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him
VIII
Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Ephesians (3:13): Brothers, I beseech you not to lose heart in my tribulations for you, which is your glory, etc.
EXPOSITION OF LUCULENTIUS.

The apostle Paul saw his course being completed, the images of the gods reduced to nothing, the prince of the world cast out, the faith of believers sprouting, the Church being built and growing, and himself cruelly persecuted because of the urgency of his labour and of the preaching of the office he had received for building up the Church. The disciples whom he had earlier taught by words he wished to instruct by examples, when he says: I BESEECH YOU NOT TO LOSE HEART IN MY TRIBULATIONS; as if to say: All that I suffer, by which I am pressed, by which I am afflicted, my tribulation is your glorying, because disciples are made firm in faith when their master suffers and is distressed for their sake. What he says can also be understood otherwise: I beseech you not to lose heart in my tribulations for you; as if it were said: Just as I do not waver amid the storms and persecutions of this world, so you too, if it should happen, do not fear the punishments set before you for the name of Christ. Rightly he says, WHICH IS YOUR GLORY. Like this is: If you suffer anything for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. FOR THIS REASON I BEND MY KNEES TO THE FATHER OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST. Here too the sense of the preceding matter fits, that the Apostle prays for the Ephesians that they may not lose heart in tribulations, when he says: For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as there are knees of the outer man, so there are also of the inner. Something of the kind the same apostle says to the Philippians: That at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things in heaven, on earth and below the earth. This certainly does not refer only to bodily kneeling. For many seem to pray with neck erect, yet before God they bend the knee humbly. And on the other hand some, praying at length, plant the knee humbly before men, [but] before God hold the neck erect. Paul, however, prayed not so much with bent knee as with the affection of the mind, when he said: For this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, FROM WHOM ALL FATHERHOOD IN HEAVEN AND ON EARTH IS NAMED. The apostle Paul says that the honour of fatherhood is named in heaven and on earth. In heaven, namely among the angelic powers, because just as we on earth, out of reverence and for the sake of veneration, name our forebears fathers, the patriarchs and prophets, so too the worthier powers in the heavens hold fatherhood. For those of the lesser order are called angels; archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers have fatherhood. And therefore the apostle Paul says: From whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named. And note that he did not say from whom it is born, but from whom it is named; as if to say: [from] that Lord who left the saints an example of so doing.

THAT HE MAY GRANT YOU, ACCORDING TO THE RICHES OF HIS GLORY, TO BE STRENGTHENED WITH POWER THROUGH HIS SPIRIT. His riches are, namely, the gifts of graces, the gifts of virtues, which he bestows on the saints, as one of those who had received [them] said: We have received from his fullness grace for grace. The apostle prays for the Ephesians, saying: That he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit. As if to say: May you be supported by such great gifts of virtues that you remain strong amid persecutions, which no one at all will be able to do unless he has been imbued with the grace of the Holy Spirit. And so he says, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit; for whoever has the Spirit of God dwelling in him will be strong and will have virtues. IN THE INNER MAN, THAT CHRIST MAY DWELL THROUGH FAITH IN YOUR HEARTS. In this he wishes to show that there are two men in one man, namely the outer, who is corrupted, [and] the inner, who is renewed from day to day, as he himself says in another place: Though our outer man is corrupted, yet the one who is within is renewed from day to day. For Christ dwells in the inner man, and this only through faith. For without faith it is impossible to please God; and conversely, The just man lives by faith. For whoever has perfect faith has Christ dwelling in him. Indeed the Father also says: And I will dwell in them, and walk among [them].

ROOTED AND GROUNDED IN CHARITY, THAT YOU MAY BE ABLE TO COMPREHEND WITH ALL THE SAINTS WHAT IS THE BREADTH, LENGTH, HEIGHT AND DEPTH. He is rooted and likewise grounded in charity whom neither prosperity lifts up nor adversity disturbs. Such was he who said: Who shall separate us from the charity of God? — 'no one' is understood. But many seem rooted in charity yet are not grounded, whom prosperity lifts up [and] adversity disturbs, who in time of peace seem to believe, in time of adversity deny; as the Lord says of false believers: Not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven. And Paul: Who profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds. The blessed apostle Paul prays for the Ephesians that they might be rooted and grounded in charity, and might be able with all the saints to comprehend what is the breadth, height and depth; not of worldly wisdom, which is foolishness with God, but of spiritual [wisdom], which is the friend of God. For the wise of this world are accustomed to comprehend the expanses of the earth: the breadth, namely, from the north to the south, the length from the rising of the sun to its setting, the height from the earth to heaven, the depth down to the abyss; counting even the drops of the Ocean sea, the number of the sands of that same sea, the stars of heaven; and this is folly. But let us, with the apostle Paul, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height and depth. First, considering the cross of our Redeemer, in which mysteries are signified. For there were breadth, length and depth first, and not at once height: the breadth was the beam that lay crosswise, where the hands of our Redeemer were fixed; the length that beam which was fixed by it in the ground, reaching up to the breadth, on which the body of our Redeemer was stretched; the depth that which was fixed in the ground, where his feet stood. For at first the cross was made in the likeness of the letter tau, but afterwards a piece of wood was added there on which his charge was written; and this was done by the will of God, so that it might contain the full mystery in itself, so that those protected by the holy sign of the cross might remain safe from the ancient enemy. This much according to the letter.

The apostle Paul wants [us] to understand spiritually what is the breadth and the length. The breadth is charity, which is accustomed to love not only friends in God but also enemies for the sake of God, of which it is written: Your commandment is exceedingly broad. The length is perseverance in good work, of which the Lord said: Whoever perseveres to the end, he will be saved. The height is hope. For what we do not see we hope for, [and] we wait for it through patience. This those can say who dwell in mind in heavenly things, like the one who said: But our way of life is in heaven. The depth is faith, the substance of things to be hoped for, the proof of things not appearing. For someone has begun to love his neighbour, that is, every man, and never, not even in persecution, has ceased from loving him; this is breadth. He does all this for the sake of obtaining eternal life; and this is height. All these things hang upon the hidden divine mercy which always protects a man inwardly; and this is depth. But if anyone ingenious should endeavour to investigate it in another sense, let him understand what follows: TO KNOW ALSO THE CHARITY OF CHRIST, WHICH SURPASSES KNOWLEDGE, THAT YOU MAY BE FILLED UNTO ALL THE FULNESS OF GOD. For the charity of Christ is surpassing and excels all these things. What follows: NOW TO HIM WHO IS ABLE TO DO ALL THINGS MORE ABUNDANTLY THAN WE ASK OR UNDERSTAND, ACCORDING TO THE POWER THAT WORKS IN US. For no one can ask so much, and understand what he asks, as he himself can bestow, who grants that we ask, who speaks through the prophet, saying: Before you call upon me, I will hear. And in his own person he says: Without me you can do nothing.

TO HIM BE GLORY, ALSO IN THE CHURCH IN CHRIST JESUS, TO ALL GENERATIONS OF THE WORLD OF WORLDS. AMEN. To him, namely to God the Father; in the Church, that is, in the congregation of the just and faithful, who glorify him without ceasing, giving thanks to God, and this through Christ. When he says, in Christ Jesus to all generations, [he means that] through his Son the Father is praised on earth. And he rightly said, to all generations of the world of worlds. Amen. For before the Son of God had come into the world, [God] had known only one people, according to what is written: God is known in Judaea, his name is great in Israel. But after the Son of God came on earth, his teaching shone throughout the whole world. Now it is said: Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth. This is what the Apostle says: To all generations of the world of worlds. Amen. When he says of the world, he shows the form of the present time; but when he adds of worlds, he shows that God is praised in his saints without end. And therefore we ought without ceasing to give thanks to him who gave us such teaching, so that we may thus be able to know him.
IX.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Ephesians (4:1): Brothers, I, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling with which you have been called, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

In this sentence a twofold meaning is to be understood. As regards the letter, he was a prisoner in the Lord, that is, for the Lord's sake, because, preaching the faith of Christ, he could not be opposed or raised up by any persecutor, and for this reason he was thrust into prison; and this is what he says: I, A PRISONER IN THE LORD. Otherwise, he was bound in the Lord with the Ephesians by the bond of charity, of which he says in another place: But above all these things having charity, which is the bond of perfection. So the saints, once they are glued together in charity, cannot be separated. So we read of David and Jonathan: The soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David. And therefore Paul was joined to the Ephesians by such great love that not only in time of peace, but not even in persecution, did he withdraw from them; though he was absent in body, he was with them in spirit. He also entreated them to keep unshaken the faith they had received: THAT YOU WALK WORTHILY OF THE CALLING WITH WHICH YOU HAVE BEEN CALLED. As if he said: [as for] him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light, follow worthily in his footsteps, with humility, patience, obedience and the other virtues. How is this road to be walked? Namely not with the step of the feet but with the affection of the mind. For he walks worthily of the calling with which he has been called who is neither lifted up in prosperity nor cast down in adversity, nor turns aside to the right or to the left, hearing the prophet saying: This is the way, walk in it, neither to the right nor to the left. For how each of the faithful ought to walk, the Apostle at once added, as if explaining, when he says: WITH ALL HUMILITY AND MEEKNESS, WITH PATIENCE. Rightly he said first, with all humility, because whoever gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind. Of humility the Lord says: Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and the one who trembles at my words? Hence it is that Peter says: Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation. Hence again the Lord himself says: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled. And with meekness; whoever has it will offer a path not only to those of his household but also to rustics, imitating God, who says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. And again: Blessed are the meek, for they shall see God. With patience; whatever adversity befalls the faithful, they bear it all patiently; as the same apostle says in another place: In much patience. And on account of that [saying]: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. Elsewhere too it is said: In your patience you will possess your souls. This virtue the Lord, going to his passion, commended to his disciples, saying: Peace I leave you, my peace I give you.

BEARING WITH ONE ANOTHER IN CHARITY. We have expounded this sentence in the Epistle to the Galatians, at the place where it is said: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. The law of Christ is love, as he himself says: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. And therefore with patience we ought to bear with one another, so that whoever sees someone straying should call him back to the way of truth, [call] the angry to concord, raise the fallen, console the grieving, give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the cold. And so it comes about that, comforting our brothers in every need, we bear with them patiently. ONE BODY. He calls the holy Church one body, as he says in another place, that we are one body and one bread in Christ. For although the holy Church is divided into members, yet standing in the unity of faith it is one body, as the same apostle says elsewhere: You are the body of Christ, and members of members; he added: ONE SPIRIT. He shows the unanimity which all the faithful ought to have, according to what is written: Who makes those of one mind dwell in a house. Peter too admonishes, saying: Be all of one mind in prayer, compassionate. Otherwise, he says one spirit, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is divided into sevenfold graces, by whom all the faithful are signed. Thus one Spirit holds the Trinity. AS YOU WERE CALLED IN THE ONE HOPE OF YOUR CALLING. By the one hope of your calling he means heavenly blessedness, toward which all the elect tend. But the sentence of the apostle Paul seems quite contrary to the word of the Lord, where he says: In my Father's house there are many mansions. And the Apostle says: In the one hope of your calling; yet if you consider rightly, both the Lord speaks truly and the apostle Paul is truthful. In the house, says the Lord, of my Father there are many mansions; as the same [apostle] added: one in this way, another in that. And this on account of the merits of different people, because each of the saints receives his reward according as he deserves. For the Lord himself says of himself: The just will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father; yet not all equally; but, as Scripture says, star differs [from star] in brightness, so will it be in the resurrection of many [of the dead]. For the brightness of the sun is one thing, the brightness of the moon another, the brightness of the stars another; so too will it be in the resurrection of the dead, according to the reasoning stated above. Hence the angel says to the prophet Daniel: The learned will shine like the splendour of the firmament, and those who instruct many unto justice, like stars for perpetual eternities. Yet there is one hope of all the elect, namely the heavenly kingdom, where, once joined together, they cannot be separated.

ONE LORD, ONE FAITH, ONE BAPTISM, ONE LORD AND FATHER OF ALL, WHO IS ABOVE ALL, AND IN ALL THINGS. There is one Lord, that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, who is not divided but always stands in unity. And one faith of believers, and likewise one baptism, as the Lord himself says: Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. It must be carefully weighed why the Apostle says one baptism. So Luke too testifies in the Acts of the Apostles when he says: The baptism which John preached, how the Lord anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. For there is one baptism, which is attested to be given in the Trinity; as the Lord himself says in another place: John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit. And therefore there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all things, AND IN US ALL. God the Father is said to be one; and he rightly says Father of all, because [he is] Father of all creatures, according to what is written: He who abides for ever created all things together.

Since mention of the Trinity has been made here, it remains for us to say something more precisely about it. For he said first, one Spirit; then one Lord; third, one God and Father of all. He placed first the Holy Spirit, then the Son, third the Father. This testimony is used against Arius and those like him, who had said: the Father is greater, the Son lesser, the Holy Spirit much lesser than the Father and the Son. For the one whom he called much lesser, the Apostle placed first when he says, one Spirit. And again, the one whom he called lesser than the Father he placed in the second place, when he said, one God and Father of all, who is above all and through all things. And not only Paul, but also holy David, fortifying [Cod.: foreseeing] the Holy Spirit and the faith and honour of the holy Trinity against heretical perversity, distinguishes thus: Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts. By saying right spirit, he shows the Holy Spirit. And when he adds: Do not cast me away from your face, he speaks of the Son. And when he goes on: Restore to me the joy of your salvation, he certainly points to the Father. And note that Paul says: Who is God above all, blessed for ever; not who are gods, but who is God. For he prudently distinguished the Trinity, but faithfully united it when he said: who [is] above all, that is, God the Father; and above all things, God the Son. For in him, says the Apostle, we live, move and are. And in all, the Holy Spirit, who going and circling about fills the hearts of the faithful, according to what is written: You know that you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you, who is blessed for ever; in every creature, in which God is praised and blessed, as is written in the hymn of the three youths: Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord; praise and exalt him above all for ever.
X.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Ephesians (4:23): Brothers, be renewed in the spirit of your mind, etc.
EXPOSITION OF LUCULENTIUS.

The Apostle commanded [them] to be renewed in the spirit of your mind, of which [he says] elsewhere: Though our outer man is corrupted, yet the one who is within is renewed. And he rightly says: BE RENEWED IN THE SPIRIT OF YOUR MIND; because we are renewed neither in understanding without spirit, nor in spirit without understanding. For just as we sing psalms with the spirit, let us sing psalms with the mind too; we pray with the spirit, let us pray with the mind too; so we ought to be renewed in understanding, so that when it has been cleansed and purged, a renewed spirit may also be joined to it. Whoever does this, his spirit is no longer called simply spirit, but is said to be the spirit of understanding. AND PUT ON THE NEW MAN, WHO HAS BEEN CREATED ACCORDING TO GOD. This seems to me to be the same as what he says elsewhere too: Put on Christ Jesus, since all the faithful put on Christ, and it is said to them by the Apostle: As many of you as believed have put on Christ. For the saints too are sometimes called the clothing of the Lord, as he says elsewhere: As I live, says the Lord, you shall be clothed with all these as with an ornament. And the saints put on the Lord when they renew the spirit of their mind. And he rightly calls the Lord Jesus the new man, because he came as a new man into the world, and gave new precepts to the world. For new was his conception, birth, nativity, baptism, teaching, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension into the heavens. Whatever you consider in him, in the man he assumed there was nothing but newness. For he who existed as God in his own [nature] before the ages, at the end of the age appeared as a new man in ours. This new man the new men ought to put on by imitating him, so that they may be gentle, meek, humble, merciful, not returning evil for evil or curse for curse, and by fulfilling the like things that he commands. Those who do this put on the new man Christ, and are able to say: But I live, now not I, but Christ lives in me, WHO HAS BEEN CREATED ACCORDING TO GOD.

Note that in the sacred Scriptures the word is found used not of the least but of the highest and most eminent creations. For example: the world was created, the house was built, the city was founded. Consider the order, and see the greatness of the man assumed by God. He is said to be created, as it were, as the world [was]. For he who before the ages existed as God together with the Father, as you have in Wisdom: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, at the end of the ages was created new, a new man according to God. But this seems contrary to our faith, which we confess saying: The Son is from the Father alone, not made, not created, but begotten. But always, as has often been said, we must understand two natures in the Son of God, namely the divine and the human: the divine, in which he is equal to the Father, in which he was neither made nor created; the human, in which he was born of a mother as man. He sets out the order of how: IN JUSTICE AND HOLINESS AND TRUTH. Jesus, then, the Son of God, was created in justice and holiness, because he is God, the Son of the true God. And note: religion and justice were fulfilled in him together with truth; and therefore [he says] well in justice, because he had no stain of sin; just, because he loves justice; holy, as he himself says: Be holy, for I too, the Lord your God, am holy. And truth, when he says: I am the way, the truth and the life.

WHEREFORE, PUTTING AWAY LYING, SPEAK TRUTH EACH ONE WITH HIS NEIGHBOUR. Because you ought to put on the new man, you ought first to put away lying and to speak the truth. Similar is what holy David says to the sinner: Turn away from evil, and do good. And the same apostle to Titus: That we should deny ungodliness and worldly desires. Peter to the dispersed (1 Pet. 3:10): He who wishes to love life and to see good days, let him restrain his tongue from evil. So here too: putting away lying. Lying is every deceitful word. Augustine says that every lie is a sin. Hear another [text] too: You hate all who work iniquity. By neighbour in this place we must not understand only a blood relation, or a kinsman, or a neighbour, but every man; otherwise, ought the one who is not a neighbour to hear a lie? Certainly not. For if we must understand neighbour only as a blood relation or kinsman, what shall we do about what is said elsewhere: You shall not commit adultery with your neighbour's wife? If you understand neighbour only as a blood relation, he seems to give them licence to lie with women who are strangers. And truly all adulterers go to punishment: and fornicators and adulterers God will judge. Therefore by neighbour must be understood every man, with whom, lying abandoned, it is necessary to speak the truth. FOR WE ARE MEMBERS OF ONE ANOTHER. Here a distinction is made, so that you understand neighbour as every man. But one cannot be a member except as faithful to faithful. For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what part has the faithful with the unbeliever? None, is understood. So neither can a pagan be a member to a Christian, but only those to whom the Apostle says: You are the body of Christ, and members of members.

BE ANGRY, AND DO NOT SIN. Anger is twofold, not only among us but also among the philosophers. For there is an anger which befalls man naturally, when the mind is stirred to fury, of which the prophet [says]: My eye is troubled by fury. This he could not forbid altogether, and therefore he says: Be angry, and do not sin. But there is also another anger which comes down from the spite of envy, from which strife and hatred are born, which he counts in the catalogue of vices, saying: Angers, strifes, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revellings. LET NOT THE SUN GO DOWN UPON YOUR WRATH. If we understand simply this sun which we see with bodily eyes, licence seems to be given us to be angry through the day. And what shall we do? For a man can sin in one day as much as he cannot repent of in the course of years. Therefore [it is said] not of this sun, but of the sun that is Christ, who sets for the wicked, according to what is said of the false prophets: The sun has set for them at midday; but rises for the saints, according to what is said: For you who fear the name of the Lord the sun of justice shall rise. And this is what is said: Let not the sun go down upon your wrath. As if he were saying: if, with the mind stirred, anger has crept in, turn quickly to repentance, lest the soul, suddenly snatched away, be darkened, or the sun of justice, or the ruling part of the heart, be wrapped in darkness. It can also be understood as said simply of this sun, according to what David says in the fourth psalm, from which it seems to be taken: What you say in your hearts, be sorry for upon your beds; that is, whatever you transgress during the day in thought, anger, or deeds, be sorry for upon your beds. Return to peace before sunset, and do not put it off until the morrow. DO NOT GIVE PLACE TO THE DEVIL. Devil, then, as a name, is in Latin called accuser; in the Hebrew tongue he is called Satan, adversary or opponent; by the Apostle he is named Belial, that is, without yoke, because he has thrown off servitude from his neck; Aquila translated him apostate. We must not give place to him by sinning, by being angry; for the devil's place is sin. He seeks a place daily by going about, as the apostle Peter says: Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. And this because he envies every good. For by the envy of the devil death entered into the world.

LET HIM WHO STOLE STEAL NO LONGER. The apostle Paul calls theft every harm done to a neighbour; for the lovers of this world, embracing the riches of the present time, envy their neighbours, seize by force, or cheat them in business and take [their goods] away; therefore he admonishes the Ephesians not to incur the crime of theft on the occasion of gain. Hence he says to other disciples: Let not the greedy man defraud his brother in business. What he says, let him who stole steal no longer, can also be understood more deeply; namely as was said of the false prophets, that each stole words from his neighbour; and as many as came were thieves and robbers. All such steal the word of God and speak lies with their neighbour. And such as these he forbids to commit theft, according to what he also said above: Putting away lying, speak truth each one with his neighbour. BUT RATHER LET HIM LABOUR, WORKING WITH HIS HANDS WHAT IS GOOD. Similar is what has already been said: Turn away from evil, and do good. And he rightly says working with the hands what is good, so that he who before seized another's goods by theft may begin to bestow his own. The same must be understood of other matters too. And note: he did not say, let him labour, working with his hands what is good, so as to have a living and not be in need, or be a burden to no one; but let him labour, he says, THAT HE MAY HAVE SOMETHING TO GIVE TO HIM WHO SUFFERS NEED. For he who labours for himself, so as not to be in need himself, does not yet fulfil the Apostle's precept. Therefore let him labour, working with his hands: because, as has often been said, every man [should be] as ready to do good [as ...]. If he cannot be readier, at least as it were in measure [So the passage stands in the Cod.], as the same apostle says elsewhere: For as you yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members in sanctification. From his own labour [let him] feed the hungry, or give drink to the thirsty, and help in the other things he sees them to need. Or especially let him work in the field of his own soul, that it may be filled with spiritual loaves, and he may be able to give food in due season to his fellow servants, on account of that [saying]: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward, whom the lord has set over his household, to give them food in due season?
XI.
Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to the Ephesians (v, 15): Brethren, see therefore how you walk circumspectly, not as unwise, but as wise, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

It has often been said that, just as there are outer eyes of the body, with which we see this light, so there are also inner [eyes] of the heart, with which God is seen, of which he himself says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. And just as there are outer steps of the body, so there are also inner [steps] of the mind, of which it is written: The steps of man are directed by the Lord. What he says here: SEE THEREFORE HOW YOU WALK CIRCUMSPECTLY, is like what the Saviour says: Walk while you have the light. For just as, to give an example, a man making a journey looks ahead to where he may set the step of his foot, so he who desires to walk spiritually must look ahead to where he may set the step of his mind, lest he fall. Therefore each one must walk circumspectly, lest he fall, and not turn aside to the right or to the left; but let him go forward safe through the armour of justice, hearing the prophet's warning: This is the way, walk in it. He who does this will be able to say: Your word is a lamp to my feet, Lord, and a light to my paths. REDEEMING THE TIME, BECAUSE THE DAYS ARE EVIL. He means that time which we all lost in Adam, namely immortality and the blessedness of paradise. For it must be known that he had been created immortal by God, if he had not sinned. It would not have been necessary to redeem the time, because, made citizens of heaven, we would behold God face to face, as he himself did before he sinned. But if anyone wishes to redeem the time, let him hear the counsel of the Lord, who says: If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also. And again: Pray for those who persecute and slander you. And this is what he says: Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. For we redeem the time when we bring our past life back to memory, and punish with weeping the things we committed through negligence, which the wicked never do, as the prophet says: Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days. Because the days are evil. As far as reason and spiritual understanding are concerned, the days were made good by God, as Scripture says: God saw all that he had made, and they were very good. You have it written in the book of Genesis that God created all things over intervals of days. And it is said there: God saw all that he had made, and they were very good. If, then, all that God made was very good, then the days too were good. But they were corrupted by the vice of men, and the days became evil. And what shall I say? Since Adam sinned in paradise, there have never been any days but evil ones. Children are born, they begin with weeping and misery; these become the evil days of their calamity. The prophet lamented these when he said: Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged! These days we must redeem by abstaining, fasting, praying, keeping vigil, and fulfilling the other things the Lord commanded. He who does this redeems the evil days, and makes good days, not of the present time, but of the future; so much so that it is no longer called days in the plural number. Of which the prophet [says]: Better is one day in your courts than thousands.

THEREFORE DO NOT BECOME IMPRUDENT. That man is imprudent who does not look ahead for himself to the way by which he ought to step, so as not to stumble, but to walk circumspectly. Not as unwise, but as wise. He is imprudent who does not redeem the time and the evil days granted to him for repentance, of which the Apostle [says]: Do you not know that the patience of God awaits you for repentance? He is imprudent who does not understand WHAT IS THE WILL OF GOD, good, and well-pleasing, and perfect. And therefore he says: Therefore do not become imprudent. The will of God is that one should turn aside from evil and do good. For the prophet says: I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live. And again: Turn aside from evil and do good. The will of God is that we love one another: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. The will of God is that we all be holy, as he himself says: Be holy, for I am holy. AND DO NOT BE DRUNK WITH WINE, IN WHICH IS LUXURY. For just as a man cannot serve two masters, namely God and mammon, so no one can be drunk with wine and at the same time be filled with the Holy SPIRIT. He who has been filled with the Holy Spirit will have prudence, chastity, purity, modesty, meekness, bashfulness. On the other hand, he who is drunk with wine will have wantonness, folly, recklessness, frenzy, lust. And therefore the Apostle commands that one must not be drunk with wine, in which is luxury. Hence Solomon also says: Do not look at wine when it turns golden in the glass; for its colour enters pleasantly [Cod., pleasant], but it bites like a serpent. What he says can also be understood otherwise: Do not be drunk with wine, that is, with the wine of malice, of which Moses [speaks] in the song in Deuteronomy: From the vineyard of Sodom is their vine. With this wine all lovers of the world are made drunk. Of whom the Apostle says: Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.

SPEAKING TO YOURSELVES IN PSALMS, AND HYMNS, AND SPIRITUAL SONGS. He who abstains from wine and is filled with the Holy Spirit will be able to be filled [with] all these things in full [So the Cod.]. Psalms, and hymns, and songs are found in the psalter; but between a psalm and a hymn there is this difference, that the psalm pertains to the body, because through the instrument of the body one learns how to arrive at the instrument of the mind; the hymn, however, pertains to prayer; the song to the praise of God. But if you wish to understand more deeply, the psalm pertains to the body, the hymn to the praise of God, the song to the strength and power of God. And note that when he says psalms, hymns, and songs, he added spiritual, which he certainly would not have done unless there were songs that are not spiritual, such as the poems of poets, the sayings of philosophers, lustful songs, and words that move laughter, which are beside the point, and buffoonery. SINGING IN GRACE IN YOUR HEARTS. Let the boys hear this, let the young men hear it, and every ecclesiastical order to whom the office of chanting has been entrusted in the Church, so that as they chant with the mouth, they may learn to chant with the heart also, lest it be said of them: This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. On the contrary, many chant with the heart and do not chant with the mouth. They cry out with the heart, they are silent with the mouth. As he did to whom it is said: Why do you cry out to me? And certainly it is not written there what Moses had cried out; but he was crying out, and crying out with the heart, and therefore God says to him: Why do you cry out to me? Therefore it is better to chant with the heart and be silent with the mouth than to be silent with the heart and chant with the mouth. And therefore let him who chants with the mouth chant with the heart also; let us chant with the spirit, let us chant also with the mind.

GIVING THANKS TO THE LORD. This sentence can be understood in two ways, that is, in things received and lost, as Job says: The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it was done; blessed be the name of the Lord. Or in prosperity and adversity. Hence it is sung in the psalm: I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise shall be always in my mouth. Otherwise: if you have the office of chanting in the church, you must not on that account exalt yourself above the others, but rather give thanks to God, saying with the Psalmist: Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. TO GOD AND THE FATHER, BEING SUBJECT TO ONE ANOTHER IN THE FEAR OF CHRIST: to God, that is, to the Son of God, who, though he was God, deigned to become man, taking on our humanity; and therefore, namely, to the Father, being subject to one another. Let bishops, priests, and all who preside in the Church hear this, that just as the others are subject to them, so they themselves may through charity be subject to their own, as Solomon exhorts [Cod., prays]: Have they made you a ruler? Do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them. And the apostle Paul says: Though I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all; and this IN THE FEAR OF CHRIST, fearing lest we do anything contrary to his will, or for the sake of men's favour or praise, lest it be said of us: They have received their reward; but let us do everything for the love of Christ, as the Apostle admonishes: Whether you eat, or drink, or do anything else, do all in the name of the Lord. And again: Whatever you do in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord. And this is what he says: in the fear of Christ.
XII.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Ephesians (6:10): Brothers, for the rest, be strengthened, and in the might of his power, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

For above, the apostle Paul had admonished the men separately and the women separately, masters and servants, sons and fathers, saying: Men, love your wives, just as Christ also [loved] the Church. Let wives be subject to their husbands; sons, obey your parents in all things, for this is pleasing in the Lord. Fathers, do not provoke your sons to anger, so that they may not become faint-hearted. Servants, obey your fleshly masters, not serving to the eye as pleasing men, but rather God; and things like these. Then, gathering all into one, he says: FOR THE REST, BE STRENGTHENED IN THE LORD. For the rest, that is, for what remains. For he knew that it was written: Cursed is the man who trusts in man. And again: Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord. And therefore he says: Be strengthened in the Lord, that is, presume nothing of your own merits, and always glory in the Lord, according to what the same apostle says: He who glories, let him glory in the Lord. And the Psalmist: Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. And lest anyone should think that he ought to place his hope in the name only, he therefore added: AND IN THE MIGHT OF HIS POWER. As if he were saying: Place your hope in Christ the Lord, without whom there can be no good, and through whom all good things are bestowed, as the apostle James says: Every best gift is from above. PUT ON THE ARMOUR OF GOD, SO THAT YOU MAY BE ABLE TO STAND AGAINST THE SNARES OF THE DEVIL. For from the things that are read below, and those which the apostle Paul says here, we can understand the whole of it of Christ. For just as the belt is truth and the breastplate is justice, there is no doubt that Christ is both truth and justice; therefore he who has put on truth and justice will have put on Christ, whom anyone who wishes to fight against the devil must put on. For 'devil' is a Greek name; in Latin it is called 'accuser': this is the accuser of whom we read in the Apocalypse that the saints said to God: We give you thanks, because the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before the sight of our God. According to the Hebrew truth it is interpreted 'flowing downward'; he wishes to strike us invisibly with his darts, and against him invisible arms must be taken up to resist him.

FOR OUR WRESTLING IS NOT AGAINST FLESH AND BLOOD. Flesh and blood sometimes signifies vices, sometimes sins, sometimes kinship, sometimes the propagation of the human race, sometimes persecuting men, of whom Paul speaks in this place: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, BUT AGAINST PRINCES AND POWERS. But rather he wishes to show that the persecutors themselves have the devil as their author, against whom invisible arms must be taken up, so that, he being destroyed, we may not fear men. For there is a wrestling against flesh and blood when the flesh lusts against the spirit. Namely, from this example we can gather that when the flesh itself lusts against the spirit, it is only by the instigation of the devil, since our wrestling is not, etc. For if you go through the series of the Old and New Testament by reading, you will nowhere be able to find demons called princes and powers, except first in this place. By this name the Apostle therefore wrote to the Ephesians about invisible creatures, wishing to show them many things. And because they had senses trained to understand even hidden things, he therefore told them beforehand various names for invisible creatures. For he said: Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against princes and powers, AGAINST THE RULERS OF THE WORLD OF THIS DARKNESS. For by princes and powers, rulers of the world, he means the demons who are greater. But there are demons of a lesser order. Just as, of the angelic dignities, we speak of angels and archangels, on account of the lesser rank of the lower ones, so we call demons principalities and powers on account of the malice of their crimes. For the more cunning they are in urging malice, the greater they seem to be. To give an example, those demons are evil by whom murders are committed, worse those by whom fratricides and parricides [are committed]. So too of adulteries and incests, of which the prophet says: They have been led astray by a spirit of fornication. These he calls princes and powers, these rulers of the world of this darkness, these he names SPIRITS OF WICKEDNESS [In Cod., consistently, wickedness] IN THE HEAVENLY PLACES. He calls the demons rulers of the world; hence also the Lord: Now the prince of the world will be cast out. He was the first angel, who fell from heaven through pride. Him [Scripture] reproaches, saying: How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who rose in the morning? You have fallen, you who wounded the nations? He is the angel of darkness, of whom Paul says: Who, though he is an angel of darkness, transformed himself into an angel of light. He is the ruler of the world, namely of all lovers of the world, who love the world. For of these the devil is ruler and rider alike; and all sinners, [who are] darkness, are sometimes changed and become light, as is said of them: You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord; and Christ becomes their ruler, and it is said of them: Whoever are led by the spirit of God, these are sons of God. Against the spirits of wickedness in the heavenly places. For he who dwells in the heavenly places was a spirit of wickedness. Although they had lost blessedness and forfeited their brightness, they did not lose their subtlety, and therefore he says in the heavenly places, because they are in the heavens, those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: The birds of heaven ate it up. I do not mean the ethereal or starry heaven, but the airy one, wherever the birds of heaven fly. This heaven, which is midway between heaven and earth, is said to be full of spiritual wickedness. And therefore we must overcome the spirits of wickedness for the sake of heavenly things, that is, we must fight, because the kingdom of heaven suffers violence.

THEREFORE TAKE UP THE ARMOUR OF GOD, SO THAT YOU MAY BE ABLE TO RESIST IN THE EVIL DAY, AND TO STAND PERFECT IN ALL THINGS. Therefore, because your wrestling is not against flesh and blood, take up the armour of God, which the apostle Paul has enumerated in what follows. So that you may be able to resist in the evil day. By the evil day he means the present time, of which it was said above: Redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Or the day of judgement, of which the prophet says: That day is a day of wrath. So that you may be able to resist in the evil day, take up the armour of God, that is, gird yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ. And to stand perfect in all things: namely, through the arms of justice on the right and on the left. STAND THEREFORE WITH YOUR LOINS GIRDED IN TRUTH, AND CLOTHED WITH THE BREASTPLATE OF JUSTICE. For now he begins to set out what the armour of God is, which he had commanded above to be put on. And what else ought he to have put first in the armour of God than the belt? To give an example: if a warrior going against the enemy needs a belt, so that loose garments may not become a hindrance and he fall before the eyes of his enemy, so assuredly it is necessary that your loins be girded in chastity, of which I think the Lord spoke in the Gospel: Let your loins be girded. For this is why John wore a leather girdle about his loins, so that he might not be defiled by a flow of seed. Hence Solomon said: There are three things that go well, and a fourth walks happily: the lion, strongest of beasts, will fear the encounter of none; the cock girded about the loins; and the ram, and there is no king who can resist him. The cock girded about the loins signifies holy preachers, who restrain the flow of luxury in their members. Stand therefore with your loins girded in truth, that is, fortified with chastity, so that you may not fall before the enemies.

AND YOUR FEET SHOD IN THE PREPARATION OF THE GOSPEL OF PEACE. For just as there are outer members, namely hands, eyes, hearing, smell and touch, so there are also inner ones. And note that he called a certain power of the soul feet, because outer feet, unless they are shod, stumble against a stone or a thorn and cannot make their way unhindered. So the feet of our soul, unless they are shod with the hides of dead animals, that is, fortified by the example of the ancient fathers, cannot run rightly and without stumbling in the way of God's commandments. Rightly he says of the Gospel of peace, of which Scripture says elsewhere: How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news! Clothed with the breastplate of justice. For a breastplate is woven of many little rods; so a man supported by many virtues, clothed inwardly with the breastplate of justice, will be unharmed by every zeal of the enemy. IN ALL THINGS TAKING UP THE SHIELD OF FAITH. Just as above we began to weave [an account] of arms, so now something must be said about the shield. For if any man is girded, clothed with a breastplate, and has his feet shod, and goes against his enemy without a shield, he falls wounded by lances or arrows, like a stag; but if he has a shield, he will be able to throw off the enemy's darts this way and that. Spiritually, however, by the shield we can understand faith, which the soldier of Christ ought to have in full: whoever has it will be able to destroy his enemy, that is, the devil, so far as to sink him in the sea; as the Lord says: If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, Pass into the sea, and it would obey you. WITH WHICH YOU MAY BE ABLE TO EXTINGUISH ALL THE FIERY DARTS OF THE MOST WICKED ONE. The darts of the devil are to be understood as his javelins, such as gluttony, drunkenness, revellings, adulteries, and things like these. And he well said fiery, since the arrows of the devil are fiery. For all these we can extinguish through charity, which is the covenant of peace, and take up THE HELMET OF SALVATION. For just as by the shield we understood faith, what can we understand by the helmet but hope? For the helmet is placed on the head, so that it may not be struck by the enemy. So spiritually we ought to fortify our head, which is the ruling part of the mind, with our helmet, that is, with firm hope, so that we may not be struck by the enemy, that is, the devil.

AND THE SWORD OF THE SPIRIT, WHICH IS THE WORD OF GOD. For he had already given the belt, he had given the breastplate, he had given the footwear, he had given the shield, but he had not yet given the sword. And what does it profit a man if he gain the whole world? [What does it profit] if he is clothed in all the armour that is listed above, and does not hold a sword in his hand? Certainly, although he may be able to avoid the enemy's darts, he will not be able to kill the enemy himself. But if he has a sword, he will not be struck by his javelins, and he will kill him. So all these things are to be understood spiritually: namely chastity, justice, charity, the teaching of the Gospel, faith and hope. Whoever has all these will remain safe from slaughter by the enemy; and if he has the sword, he will be able to lay him low: that sword, assuredly, which the Lord came to send into the world, of which he himself says: I came not to send peace, but a sword; which the saints always hold in their hand, and which is written in the plural by the Psalmist: And two-edged swords in their hands. This Paul reveals when he says: And the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God. For the word of God is sharp; it is itself the sword of which the same Paul writes elsewhere: For the word of God is living (Cod., one) and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword, and reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
XIII.

Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Philippians (1:6): Brothers, we are confident in the Lord Jesus that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Christ Jesus, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

The Philippians are Macedonians. The apostle Paul preached to them, and they held firmly to the faith they had received, and did not accept false apostles, as some did, nor did they fear the persecution of evil men. So when the apostle Paul writes the epistle, he shows nothing by way of reproof, but only exhortation, urging them to bring the faith they had received and the good work they had begun to its completion, and always to make progress. For they were so perfect that he asked them to become his imitators, and always to advance to better things, saying: WE ARE CONFIDENT IN THE LORD JESUS THAT HE WHO BEGAN A GOOD WORK IN YOU WILL COMPLETE IT UNTIL THE DAY OF CHRIST JESUS. [That is:] All my hope and confidence about you in the Lord is this, that you will bring this good which you have begun to its completion, and hold firm the teaching you received from me. For he who began a good work in you will complete it: that is, if any of you has vowed a good work, namely to serve God, let him carry it through to the day of his death. Or, he who began in you: that is, the Lord himself, who laid the foundation of faith in you, will himself give perseverance in good work. The day of Christ we should understand in two ways: in particular, the day of death, when a perfect man passes from this life to Christ; in general, the day of judgement, when we shall all stand before the judgement seat of Christ. AS IT IS RIGHT FOR ME TO THINK THIS OF ALL OF YOU. As if he were saying: Charity compels me to think this very thing of you, to understand this very thing; for charity believes all things. It is right for me to think thus of all of you, that he who has begun a good work will persevere until the day of death. For it is the custom of the saints to rejoice at the doings of the good and to grieve at those of the wicked, as Paul himself did, who said: Who is weak, and I am not weak? And elsewhere: That I may mourn many of those who have not done penance. BECAUSE I HAVE YOU IN MY HEART, AND IN MY CHAINS. For those whom charity has once joined, although they are not together in body, are nevertheless always joined in mind. And because the Philippians were perfect in good work, the apostle, absent in body, always remembered them in the secret of his breast. And this is what he says: Because I have you in my heart and in my chains. He gives the reason why when he says: AND IN THE DEFENCE AND CONFIRMATION OF THE GOSPEL: because just as he defended the Gospel of Christ, that is, the teaching of truth, so did they too, by holding it firmly and by admonishing others. THAT YOU ARE ALL PARTNERS OF MY JOY. Partnership in this place is to be understood not of the present time but of the future, that is, eternal life. Of this joy the Saviour says to the disciples: I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice. Or certainly, if one prefers to understand it of the present time, we can fit it to what the apostle James says, namely: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations. It is the custom of the saints to rejoice more than to grieve amid persecution, knowing that it is written: No one will be crowned unless he has striven lawfully.

GOD IS MY WITNESS HOW I LONG FOR ALL OF YOU IN THE BOWELS OF JESUS CHRIST. It is also the custom of the saints, when they wish to affirm something, to call upon God, who is the searcher of the heart, as their witness, as Moses [did] before the children of Israel: I call heaven and earth, he says, as witnesses today. And because the apostle Paul greatly loved the Philippians, he called God to bear witness for him, saying: For God is my witness how I long that the Lord Jesus Christ may dwell in your inmost parts: he who speaks through the prophet, saying of the saints: And I will dwell in them and walk among them. And the same apostle elsewhere: That Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts. Or certainly: I long for all of you to be within his bowels, that you may all so love him that not even amid persecutions will you be separated from his bowels. AND THIS I PRAY, THAT YOUR CHARITY MAY ABOUND MORE. I pray that you may love God with your whole heart, your whole mouth, your whole mind, your whole inmost being, IN KNOWLEDGE AND ALL UNDERSTANDING. By knowledge he means the course of the Old Testament; by understanding, the scriptures of the New Testament. Otherwise: knowledge [is] the whole course of both the Old and the New Testament; and understanding, that you may be able to understand something spiritually, for knowledge without understanding is nothing; for knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up. THAT YOU MAY APPROVE THE BETTER THINGS, AND BE SINCERE AND WITHOUT OFFENCE UNTO THE DAY OF CHRIST. He says the better things, that is, the greater. Be knowing, so that from visible things you may be able to grasp invisible ones. For just as with the food of the palate the body grows in age, so with spiritual food the understanding of the mind ought to grow.

That you may be sincere and without offence unto the day of Christ: namely with a chaste body and a pure heart, as the Apostle says of the universal Church: I have espoused you to one husband, to present a chaste virgin to Christ. For sincerity is where two agree together, namely spirit and flesh, of which the Lord says: If two of you agree on earth about anything whatever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father, says the Lord. And without offence. Without offence means without criminal action. Or certainly: be so sincere that on the day of Christ no rust of sins may appear in you, lest you be shut out from the king's bridal chamber with the foolish virgins. The day of Christ, as we have already said, we should understand as the day of death or the day of judgement, on which day whoever is without offence will be rewarded by the Lord, according to what Solomon says: Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates. FILLED WITH THE FRUIT OF JUSTICE THROUGH JESUS CHRIST, UNTO THE GLORY AND PRAISE OF GOD; that is, with the fruit of good work, of which fruit the same apostle says: The fruit of the spirit is joy, charity, peace, patience, and things like these. Whoever does this will enjoy it in eternal life; for fruit (fructus) is named from enjoying (fruendo). And no one can bear fruit except through Jesus Christ, who says: Without me you can do nothing. Unto the glory and praise of God: that God may always be glorified in us, according to what he says in another place: Let him who glories, glory in the Lord. And the praise of God: namely that God may always be praised, as the psalmist says: I will bless the Lord at all times, his praise is always in my mouth. Otherwise: unto glory, that is, bearing fruit in good work; and the praise of God, in preaching. Let there be glory in work, praise in words, so that what the Saviour says may be fulfilled in us: So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.
XIV.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Colossians (1:9): Brothers, we do not cease praying and asking for you, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

For the blessed apostle Paul had heard of the faith of the Colossians, [which came] from the love they had toward God; and he prayed that they might grow in the virtues that follow, saying: WE DO NOT CEASE PRAYING AND ASKING FOR YOU. The apostles had this custom, and we ought to keep it: that we pray for one another, both teachers for disciples and disciples for teachers. As he says in another place: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit. Now may the God of patience and comfort grant you to be of one mind toward one another according to Jesus Christ, so that with one mind and one mouth you may honour God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. And again: I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. And that disciples too ought to pray for teachers, he himself says elsewhere as well: It is profitable for you to pray for us. For we read of blessed Peter, when he was put in prison, that prayer was made without ceasing by the church to God for him. And that he did not say in the singular 'I do not cease', but in the plural 'we do not cease', [shows that] he said this both of himself and of the others who were with him. Although to pray and to ask are one thing, there is this difference: we speak of praying about lighter matters, but of asking about greater and more difficult ones. By praying [we ask] that those who stand may not fall; by asking, that those who lie [fallen] may rise. We must pray that the just be rewarded; we must ask that the wicked be justified. THAT YOU MAY BE FILLED WITH THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE WILL OF GOD. First we must seek what God is, according to the voice of the psalmist, who says: Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always. Then [comes] the knowledge of his will, what God wills, as the same apostle says: That you may prove what is the good and well-pleasing and perfect will of God. Concerning which [so the manuscript], how we may serve God, which we cannot do unless we do his will. IN ALL WISDOM AND SPIRITUAL UNDERSTANDING. All wisdom and understanding and working, namely because it is impossible to please God without faith; so too faith without works is dead. All wisdom is not only to know the history of the Old Testament, but also to come to know its spiritual understanding. THAT YOU MAY WALK WORTHILY OF GOD, PLEASING [HIM] IN ALL THINGS. He speaks of walking not only with the body but with the mind: walking from virtue to virtue. He walks worthily who lives rightly and draws others by good example, according to that [saying]: Let him who hears say: Come. He pleases God in all things who fulfils what is added: BEARING FRUIT IN EVERY GOOD WORK, AND GROWING IN THE KNOWLEDGE OF GOD. He did not say 'in one' but 'in every'; he does not say 'standing firm for a time', but 'bearing fruit and growing in the knowledge of God', that is, that we may know how to give thanks to him for all good things, according to that [saying]: By the grace of God I am [what I am]; and: Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory. For it is his [work] to perfect us IN ALL VIRTUE. All virtue is the gift of God, who can bestow all things. All virtue belongs both to the mind and to the body. Strengthened by whom? By none but the Lord. Hence he also says elsewhere: Who also has strengthened you to the end without crime. ACCORDING TO THE MIGHT OF HIS GLORY, that is, according to his power, as the Psalmist says: I will keep my strength for you. Hence the Lord says: Without me you can do nothing; [and] Your word, Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths. IN ALL PATIENCE, that is, with neighbours and subordinates and strangers, and those who persecute us. AND LONGSUFFERING, so that we may always be patient, in adversity as in prosperity. WITH JOY. Namely, that you may always rejoice in tribulations, as the apostle James admonishes: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various temptations. Or that through sufferings and tribulations you may receive the joy to come with Christ, according to the promise of him who says: Blessed are you when men curse you and persecute you and say every evil against you falsely for my sake; rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven.
XV.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Colossians (3:12): Brothers, put on, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercy, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

The Colossians, like the Laodiceans, are Asians. Having received the word of truth, they stood firm in the faith and did not receive false apostles. They were so perfect [manuscript: persecuted] that they did not need the apostle except for exhortation alone. The Apostle exhorts and admonishes them how they should put on Christ, saying: BROTHERS, PUT ON, AS THE ELECT OF GOD, BOWELS OF MERCY. Note that to other disciples he says: As many of you as have believed have put on Christ; but here he says to the Colossians: Put on, as the elect of God. As if he were saying: Put on Jesus Christ. And he rightly says 'as the elect of God, HOLY', because they had been chosen by God, as the Lord [says], saying to the disciples: You did not choose me, but I chose you. And the Apostle: Those whom he foreknew, these he also called. 'Holy' [is said] rightly, because he too is holy who says: Be holy, because I am holy. By 'bowels of mercy' he means bowels of pity, because he loved you so much that he gave no other price for you, but shed his own blood. Of which the prophet had once foretold: Through the bowels of the mercy of our God, in which the Dayspring from on high has visited us. KINDNESS. Now he begins to set out what they ought to put on, or how, when he says 'kindness'. He rightly says 'kindness', that is, benevolence, that is, that you be benevolent to all, loving [them] as yourselves. HUMILITY. After kindness follows humility. Humility is a great virtue, which has made men angels. For of it is said: He who gathers virtue without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind, and like one who gathered wages and put them into a bag with holes. And the Lord says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. MODESTY. Modesty is the same as temperance, one of the four principal virtues. For every perfect man ought to be modest, that is, temperate, not only in food and drink, on account of that [saying]: Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness, but also in thought and speech and work and in every act. PATIENCE. The perfect man ought to be patient, as the Apostle admonishes: Pursue peace and holiness. And the Lord says: In your patience you will possess your souls. And another Scripture says: A man's wisdom is known by patience. BEARING WITH ONE ANOTHER. This is the same as what he says elsewhere: Bear one another's burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ. The law of Christ is love, which we fulfil when we bear with one another. And the Lord says: By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. AND FORGIVING ONE ANOTHER. That is, pardoning each other. IF ANYONE HAS A COMPLAINT AGAINST ANOTHER. That is, if you have wronged a brother in anything, or a brother [has wronged] you, you ought to pardon one another, that is, forgive, on account of that [saying]: Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. Whoever has done this dares confidently to say in the Lord's Prayer: Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

BUT ABOVE ALL THESE THINGS, HAVING LOVE, WHICH IS THE BOND OF PERFECTION. Like this is that [saying] of the apostle Peter: Be prudent and watch in prayers; but before all things have constant mutual love among yourselves. Love is sometimes placed first among the other virtues by the apostle on account of its dignity, or meekness, because it is greater than the other virtues. But where it is placed in the last position, it is placed so not on account of smallness or diminution, as though it were lesser, but as a foundation or firm base, as he prays for the Ephesians, saying: Rooted and grounded in love; for it is the root of all virtues, without which the other virtues are reckoned vices. For just as, to give an example, a man making a bundle out of wild twigs must bind the rest together with one of them, so that they are not scattered here and there; so whoever desires to have the other virtues must have the bond of perfection, love, because, as I said, the other virtues are nothing without love. Hence the apostle says elsewhere: If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, [but] do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. AND LET THE PEACE OF CHRIST EXULT IN YOUR HEARTS. Christ is our peace, as the Apostle says: He is our peace, who has made both one. And again: May the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts and your minds. For he exults in the hearts of the saints when he makes them exult. Of which exultation the prophet says: The saints will exult in glory. Like this is what [is said] elsewhere: God has sent the Spirit of his Son into [our] hearts, crying: Abba, Father; and: The Spirit himself will bear witness to our spirit that we are sons of God.

IN WHICH YOU ALSO WERE CALLED, that is, in Christ, who called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. By one body he means the holy Church: although it is divided into parts, yet, gathered from the members of the faithful, it is one body. You are the body of Christ, says the Apostle, and members of members; and: Just as in one body we have many members. AND BE THANKFUL. That is, gracious, acceptable to all. As he also says of himself: Just as I too please all men in all things. THE WORD OF CHRIST, that is, the teaching of Christ and the Gospel of Christ, LET IT DWELL IN YOU ABUNDANTLY, so that what you understand you may fulfil in deed. For [it dwells] abundantly in anyone when he understands rightly and fulfils it in deed; superabundantly, when he dispenses it to others. On account of what the Lord says: Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has set over his household? And again: Every scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven is like a man who is a householder, who brings out of his treasure new things and old. IN ALL WISDOM, that is, in the Old and in the New Testament. For whoever accepts the New Testament and rejects the Old is not learned in all wisdom. Otherwise: in all wisdom, in the letter and in the spiritual understanding, in allegory, so that he may be able to expound spiritually what he reads. TEACHING AND ADMONISHING. Teaching others, admonishing yourselves. This is the same as what he says to other disciples: He who teaches, in teaching; he who exhorts, in exhorting. What he says there, he who teaches, in teaching, he also says here, teaching. And what [he says] there, he who exhorts, [he says] here too, admonishing YOURSELVES. Hence also to Titus: Speak these things and exhort. But in what they ought to admonish themselves he plainly disclosed when he added: IN PSALMS AND HYMNS. The psalm pertains to the body, the hymn to the mind, the canticle to fortitude...
XVI.
Reading from the Epistle of blessed Paul the apostle to Titus (2:11): The grace of God our Saviour has appeared to all men, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

Titus is interpreted 'seeking good' or 'having struggled'. He followed Paul the apostle, and was appointed by him pastor or teacher of the church, when he says: For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what is lacking and appoint bishops in the cities, as I directed you. Let everyone who seeks the good, that is, the Lord and eternal life, know that this Epistle was written to him, so that he may be instructed by it. What he says can be understood in two ways. THE GRACE OF THE SAVIOUR HAS APPEARED; that is, either the Saviour himself, of whom John [says]: We have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten of the Father. He appeared for this purpose, to give to those who believe in him the prize of eternal life, which no one will be able to attain except by the free mercy of God. Or else the grace of the holy Gospel, which has shone throughout the whole world, as the Lord commanded the disciples: Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Of which grace the prophet says: He has made grace equal to grace. And John: Of his fullness we have all received, grace for grace. TO ALL MEN, whether Jews, or all the nations who have believed in him. He appeared to them for this purpose, that, leaving the creature, they might worship the Creator. INSTRUCTING US. That is, teaching us. For one is called instructed [eruditus] who is taught, imbued and trained. Just as, on the contrary, one is called uninstructed who is brutish, because he seems to lack sense or prudence. 'To instruct' [erudire] is so called as if 'to raise up from the countryside' [a rure]. He wished to instruct us, who used to worship wood and stones; he made [us] know him. As is said to sinful Jerusalem through the prophet Jeremiah: Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest [my] soul depart from you. And well, after the tenfold teaching—what he ought to admonish the old man, what the old woman, what the virgins, what the young men, what finally the slaves—he includes all in one, saying: For the grace of our Saviour has appeared to all men, instructing us; because with him there is no difference between Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and master, circumcised and uncircumcised, male and female, but we are all one in Christ. For he is no respecter of persons, who wills all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For he calls all to his kingdom; all of us, after the offence, are to be reconciled to our Father, not through our merits, but through the grace of the Saviour, that is, of the Son. What [is this] grace of the Father, or grace of the Son? [That] by which we have been redeemed, to whom it is said through the prophet: You will save us for nothing.

THAT, DENYING UNGODLINESS. By ungodliness he means idolatry or unbelief: this is the ungodliness which the prophet Zechariah saw sitting upon a mass of lead, in the mouth of a jar. WORLDLY DESIRES he calls the works of the flesh, which the Apostle sets out: The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, luxury, the service of idols. And he adds the virtues when he says: The fruit of the Spirit is joy, peace, patience, longsuffering, goodness, kindness. So in this place he includes all vices when he says: Turn away from evil. He touches on virtue too when he says: And do good. SOBERLY. Sobriety, as is handed down by our elders, is one of the four principal virtues. The four principal virtues [are] prudence, fortitude, temperance, justice. Sobriety is the same as temperance; for there is temperance in food and drink, on account of what the Lord says: Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness. But in thought too, and speech and work, in every act of ours, we ought to be temperate, because everything that is excessive, whether it be upward or downward, will be reckoned a vice. AND JUSTLY, that is, faithfully. The just man lives by faith. Hence also John: Everyone who does justice is of God. Sharers in it are modesty, chastity and things like these. AND LET US LIVE GODLY, that is, religiously. For lest justice be immoderate, godliness must accompany it, which is a part of justice. And, as blessed Augustine says, it is understood [as] the worship of God. IN THIS WORLD, that is, in the present life, on account of what the Lord says: Whoever perseveres to the end, he will be saved. This godliness awaits THE COMING OF THE GLORY AND OF OUR SAVIOUR JESUS CHRIST, secure in its faith and work; just as, on the contrary, ungodliness dreads it. By THE BLESSED HOPE he means the heavenly homeland. For hope is the expectation of future goods. Hope [spes] is so called as if 'the foot [pes] of walking rightly'. Of which the Apostle [says]: Hope that is seen is not hope. Contrary to it is despair, which has no capacity for repentance. For as long as a man loves sin, he does not hope for future blessedness; but he awaits it confidently who obeys his precepts in all things. Of it he could not have thought more highly, so as to call it blessed, than when he said: AWAITING the blessed hope. Well [does he say] blessed hope, because eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what the Lord has prepared for those who love him. For no one can tell what that blessedness of the saints is like; considering which, John said: Now we are sons of God, and it does not yet appear what we shall be.

And the coming of the glory OF THE GREAT GOD. By the coming of the glory he means the day of judgement, when we shall all stand before the judgement seat of Christ. Well [does he say] of the great God, because he who first came humble will come great, as he himself says: When the king sits on the throne of his kingdom, all nations will be gathered before him. And again: Then they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty. Of this Peter too says: May it be found unto praise and glory and revelation of Jesus Christ our Lord and our Saviour Jesus Christ. It should be noted that in this short Epistle he has twice named the Lord Jesus God: above, where he says: The grace of our Saviour God has appeared; and here, when he says: the coming of the glory of the great God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Jesus is a proper name; it is interpreted Saviour or saving. Christ, however, is named from anointing; for chrism is interpreted anointing. He himself was ANOINTED in a special way above all with the gift of the Holy Spirit, as the prophet says: God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows. And the apostle named God twice so as to soothe his hearers the more. As it is also said in the Psalms: God, my God, look upon me. WHO GAVE HIMSELF FOR US.
