Jesus the Son of God gave himself for us, because for the salvation of the whole human race he allowed himself to be sacrificed on the altar of the cross. As the same apostle says: He delivered himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet fragrance. Why then do we blame the Jews or Judas, when the Apostle says that he delivered himself up? Yet it must be known that Judas delivered him up for avarice, the Jews for envy, God the Father for our redemption, [and] the Son delivered himself up for love of us. As John says in the Apocalypse: Who loved us, and washed us from our sins in his blood. So Judas delivered him up in one way, the Jews in another, the Father in another, and he delivered himself up in another.

THAT HE MIGHT REDEEM US FROM ALL INIQUITY. He redeemed us from all iniquity by shedding his blood for us, as the same [apostle] says: For you have been bought at a great price. And the prophet says: You were sold for nothing. From all iniquity: in baptism, where original and actual sins are forgiven; or, as has been said, by shedding his blood for us, according to the testimony cited above: Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. What John says, He has made us a kingdom for our God, priests to God the Father, the Apostle says here too. AN ACCEPTABLE PEOPLE, that is, pleasing or perfect, so that it may be accepted by God, and that what was before the devil's people is now God's people, saying with the Psalmist: But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. A PURSUER OF GOOD WORKS, that is, of virtues. As the same [apostle] says: That in all things we may show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience, in watchings, in fastings, and in love unfeigned, by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left. Therefore we ought to be pursuers of good works, so that we may grow in good works, namely in those which the Apostle lists, saying: The fruit of the Spirit is. Speak these things and exhort. Speak with words, that is, preach; exhort with examples: what you say, do first. For then speech will be fitting, if the teacher has first done what he preaches, as is written of the Lord: That Jesus began to do and to teach. But on the contrary some say greater things and are unwilling to do lesser ones, like the Scribes and Pharisees, of whom it is written: They bind heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders, but with their own finger they will [not] move them. And because the blessed apostle Paul knew that it was written, Whoever breaks one of these least commandments and teaches men so, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven, he therefore took care to exhort his disciple to fulfil first in deeds what he taught in words.
XVII.
Reading from the Epistle of the blessed apostle Paul to the Hebrews (1:1): God, who at sundry times and in many ways spoke of old to the fathers in the prophets, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

The Hebrews took their name from Heber, who was the seventh from Adam. 'Hebrew' is interpreted 'passing over', 'Hebrews' 'those passing over'; a nation which God greatly loved, so much that he says: Israel is my firstborn; and: Israel is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his crops. We read in the book of Genesis that the sons of Noah, gathered after the waters of the flood in the land of Shinar, began to build a tower, of which they said that its top would reach up to heaven, and if the flood were to overflow again they would not perish, as had those who had lived before them long ago. They did not remember what God had said to Noah: I will set my bow in the clouds of heaven, and I will remember my covenant, so that I will not destroy all flesh with the waters of a flood. For they had grown very numerous and could not live together; before they were divided into regions or lands, they wished to win for themselves an everlasting name. And they had bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar, and began to build; the author of this work was Nimrod. But God, seeing their unalterable purpose, said: Come, let us go up and confound their language there. And so it came about that those who spoke one [language] were divided into seventy-two. But the language which all had spoken before remained only in the house of Heber.

From his house, a long time after, Abraham was born, whom God greatly loved. He gave him circumcision as a seal of faith, and it was reckoned to him as justice; moreover it was promised to him that in his seed all nations would be blessed, saying in these words: In your seed all nations shall be blessed. Expounding this the Apostle says: He does not say 'and to seeds', as of many, but as of one, 'and to your seed', who is Christ. He gave him Isaac his son in his old age, whom he circumcised on the eighth day as a type of our Saviour; and Isaac [begot] Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs, who, driven by famine, went down into Egypt, where, having multiplied greatly, they were severely afflicted. But freed by a strong hand, led out of Egypt with signs and wonders, they crossed the Red Sea, were fed with manna for forty years, and their garments did not wear out. God gave them the law, the temple, the altar, the table, the loaves of proposition, the inner veil, victims, holocausts, sacrifices. Moreover he promised him that his Son would be born of the same stock. He, coming, fulfilled what the Father had promised, for he was born of their stock according to the flesh, as Paul testifies: For I say that Christ Jesus was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers. Seeing him, they did not receive him as they ought, but cast him out of the vineyard and killed him. I do not speak of all, for from them came the holy root and lump, that is, the holy apostles and the first believers; but very many remained in blindness, of whom it is written: Blindness has befallen Israel in part until the fullness of the gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. Those who remained in unbelief plundered the property of those who came to the faith, but these bore it patiently. The apostle Paul praises them: For you also had compassion on those in chains, and accepted with joy the plundering of your goods. Taking care of them, he made a collection every year, saying to the brethren: Remember the brethren who are in Jerusalem; and he sent [it] to them.

He also wrote and sent them an Epistle, in which he wished to show that all the things then done according to the letter, namely the sabbath, circumcision, the new moon, and the other things the law commanded, were all typical, and had been fulfilled spiritually at the coming of the Son of God. Of this Epistle many of the Latins say that it is not the apostle Paul's, because his name is not set as a title at its head, but Barnabas's, according to Tertullian, or Luke's, or Clement's, or that of one of the disciples of the apostles. To them it must be answered that if it is not the apostle Paul's because his name is not set as a title at its head, then neither will it be any of theirs, since none of them is found at the head. But we ought to know for certain that this Epistle is his. That he did not wish to set his name as a title at its head, he did for various reasons. The first reason was that he knew that God, his master, had laid the foundation there. Therefore he did not dare to lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. The second reason was that he had not received the office of preaching among them, but among the gentiles, as the Holy Spirit says: Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have taken them up. For each had received his own province for preaching; hence he says: He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision worked also in me among the gentiles. The third reason was that the Jews hated him, because he made void every rite of the law. For some, coming to the faith, wished both to baptize and to circumcise their sons, which Paul utterly forbade, saying: If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing; for in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love. If he had set his name as a title on it, perhaps they would not have received it, for any man not only does not receive the letter of one he hates, but does not even want to hear his name. The fourth reason was humility: knowing their pride and his own humility, he did not wish to put his name first. For this reason the blessed John too did not set [his name] at the head of his Epistle. They also say that it is not Paul's because he did not compose the other Epistles in such rhetorical language, nor support them from the Old and New Testament, in the way this one read as 'to the Hebrews' is composed. To them it must be answered that he wrote the other Epistles in a foreign tongue, but this one in his own; the others in Greek, this in Hebrew. Nor is it surprising if that written in his own tongue is more eloquent than those in Greek. For it was fitting that what he wrote in his own tongue he should compose in more brilliant language and support from the Old and New Testament. Keeping its sense and order, the evangelist Luke, after the death of the apostle Paul, put it into Greek. But now let us treat this apostolic Epistle itself, which begins thus.

AT SUNDRY TIMES AND IN MANY WAYS GOD, SPEAKING OF OLD TO THE FATHERS IN THE PROPHETS. In saying 'at sundry times' [multifarie] he shows that there was a certain prophecy concerning the Son of God. Phari in Greek is said to mean 'to speak' in Latin. He says 'multifarie', in many utterances. For in many ways the Lord spoke to the earlier fathers who were in the Old Testament: sometimes through visions, sometimes through likenesses, sometimes through [words]. Through visions, as in this: I also multiplied visions, and in the hands of the prophets I was represented. He spoke through likenesses, as is said to be found in many places; so Ezekiel, when he says: And you, son of man, dig through the wall with your hand. Through words, as to the prophet Isaiah: The word of the Lord which came to the prophet Isaiah. Through revelation, as to Daniel. Through himself, as to Abraham: Go out from your land. And to Moses: Moses spoke with God face to face. And this is what he says: At sundry times and in many ways. 'Of old' means before, that is, in the Old Testament. 'Lastly' means in the last time, in the days of the Lord's incarnation. Of which days the same Paul says: We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come. And John: Little children, it is the last hour. And again Paul: But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son. When he says: IN THESE LAST DAYS HE HAS SPOKEN TO US IN THE SON, it is as if he said: what wonder if he sent prophets to the fathers and spoke to them through them, he who has spoken to us through the Son? To them he appointed prophets; to us he sent his Son, and through him deigned to speak to us. Of whom Matthew says: He was teaching them as one having authority, not as [that] of the Scribes and Pharisees. He who once spoke through patriarchs and prophets deigned to speak through himself.

WHOM HE APPOINTED HEIR OF ALL THINGS. 'Inheritance' is named from 'master' (*herus*), that is, from God, because it is bestowed by free power. The Father appointed the Son heir of all things, that is, of the whole world, when he says: You have put all things under his feet. Hence the same Son also says: But I have been appointed king by him. So, rising from the dead, he declares that power has been given to him; as the same [says]: All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. And again: The Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son. Therefore Jacob is no longer the Lord's portion alone, nor Israel only his lot, but we embrace all peoples and nations, spread over the whole world, in the inheritance of the blood of Christ, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend; in that he was made man, he was appointed by the Father, and all things were made subject to him by him; in that he is equal to the Father, the same Son says: All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine. THROUGH WHOM HE MADE THE AGES. 'Through the Son' is understood. He uses this against the heretics who said: If Christ exists, there was a time when he was not; but in this he overthrows them when he says: Through whom he also made the ages. For what he says, 'and whom he appointed heir of all things', pertains to the humanity. But what he added, 'through whom he also made the ages', [pertains] to the divinity. For God the Father made the ages through the Son, as you have it written: In the beginning God made heaven and earth. He shows that he was with the Father before all ages, and with him founded all things. Hence John too: All things were made through him. And he himself speaks in Wisdom: The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways. For just as the Father judges no one, but is said to judge all things through the Son, whom he begot as judge, so too he is said to work through the Son, whom he is known to have begotten as maker.

WHO, BEING THE BRIGHTNESS OF GLORY. For he is the brightness of glory, that is, God from God, light from light, almighty from almighty, Son from Father, who says: I am the light. And of whom John [says]: He was the true light which enlightens every man coming into this world. AND THE FIGURE OF HIS SUBSTANCE. When you hear 'figure', do not be scandalized; for 'figure' or 'character' in this place you must understand not as likeness but as truth. [It is] as if you saw an image painted on a wall and said: Look, a man, look, hands, look, feet. But the image is one thing, you another: it by likeness, you in truth. AND BEARING ALL THINGS BY THE WORD OF HIS POWER. The Word and the truth is Christ, of whom Paul [says]: Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. And of whom John [says]: In the beginning was the Word. When the Apostle says of the Son of God that he bears all things, he destroys the madness of the Arians, who say that the Father commanded, saying: Let there be light, and the Son obeyed; for he shows that he accomplished all things by his own word. 'Bearing', he says, 'all things', that is, governing. For he holds together things that are falling and tending to nothing. For just as he created all things out of nothing without any labour, according to what is written: He who abides for ever created all things together; so he rules and holds together and bears all things without labour. For in him we live, move and are, and all things hold together in him, as the same apostle says elsewhere. For nothing could subsist unless he held all things together through himself. And this is what the Son himself says to the Jews: My Father works until now, and I work. For he was sent as much to govern the world as to create [it]. For when the world was created, all things were made out of nothing so that they might be. But in governing, the work is that the things which are should not be reduced to nothing nor perish.

MAKING PURGATION OF SINS. For after the apostle showed that the Son governed and held together all the things he made, he wished also to make plain his care, his mercy, which he showed towards us, saying: Making purgation of sins. For he made purgation of sins when, as he hung on the cross, his side was opened and blood and water flowed for our redemption, as the apostle says: For you were bought at a great price. And this: Who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. Of this purgation of sins it is said through Peter: Who himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree. He makes purgation of sins daily through baptism, of which it is said: As many of you as have believed have put on Christ. He also makes purgation of sins when he gives his body and blood to his faithful to eat, he who says: I am the living bread which came down from heaven; and: My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. And again: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you. And: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him. For when about to go to his passion he said to the disciples: This is my body, which will be given up for you for the remission of sins. For just as fire melts wax, and as flame burns up straw, so lesser sins through participation in the body and blood of Christ
XVIII.
Reading from the First Epistle of the blessed apostle Peter (5:6): Dearly beloved, humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation, etc.
COMMENTARY OF LUCULENTIUS.

For humiliation is understood [as] the last; for each one ought to humble himself by fasting, praying, obeying, patiently enduring adversities, because of what is written: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. The apostle Peter commands us to be humbled, saying: HUMBLE YOURSELVES UNDER THE MIGHTY HAND OF GOD. For humility is a manifold grace. We ought to be humble because of what the Lord says: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. And elsewhere: Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one, and him who trembles at my words? Under the mighty hand of God. For the hand of God is sometimes understood as the Son, sometimes as divine protection. The Son is understood as the hand, as in that saying of the prophet: Send forth your hand from on high. Divine protection, as in this: The hand of the Lord came upon me. But in this place divine protection is understood, as the psalmist testifies: You have protected me, O God, from the assembly of the wicked. Under his hand we ought to be humbled, that is, under divine protection, so that he may deign to exalt us on the day of visitation. AND IN THE TIME OF VISITATION; that is, on the day of judgement, when all the humble will deserve to be exalted and the proud to be humbled, as was said above: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. And all the reprobate together with their head will be cast into hell. CASTING ALL YOUR SOLICITUDE UPON HIM, FOR HE HAS CARE OF YOU. Similar is what the Psalmist says: Cast your thought upon the Lord. And the Lord in the Gospel: Do not be solicitous, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink? For your Father knows what you need. Therefore we ought to cast all our solicitude upon him from whom we believe every good is bestowed. And whatever is perfect, whatever is good that a man does, he receives from him, as James testifies, who says: Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above. And elsewhere it is written: Who has hoped in the Lord and been put to shame?

BE SOBER. For sobriety is to be understood not only of the body but also of the soul. For just as the outer man ought to be sober, namely sparing in food and drink, because of what the Lord says: Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness; so the inner man [ought to be sober] in vigils, fasts and prayers, and other good works. AND WATCH justly. We ought to watch because of what is written: And watch justly, and do not sin. And the Lord in the Gospel: Watch, lest your flight be in winter or on the sabbath. And again: But know this, that if the householder knew at what hour the thief would come, he would certainly watch. But in this place why we ought to watch is shown next: FOR YOUR ADVERSARY THE DEVIL, AS A ROARING LION, GOES ABOUT SEEKING WHOM HE MAY DEVOUR. For the devil is the adversary and enemy of the human race, who from the beginning of the world has never ceased to persecute the saints, and strives to scatter the folds of the faithful. The devil is called a lion not for strength but for savagery; for he not only lies in wait secretly but also rages openly. He lies in wait secretly, for sometimes he persuades someone through wicked thoughts, through gluttony, through drunkenness, through avarice; he trips [him] up with anger, or defiles [him] with luxury. But against another he rages like a lion and openly persecutes the man, as the apostle Peter says here: Your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. For the devil goes around each one of us, looking out for an entrance through which he may break in and deceive, and in whatever part he sees one more prone to sin, there he burns the more fiercely. Namely, or through the right hand; for in tempting a man to greater vices, if he cannot prevail to deceive him, he brings on lesser ones, and from the good he sees he instils pride, so as to enter thus through the right side. For, as I said at the beginning, from the time that the first just man Abel was slain by his brother Cain through envy, down to the last saint who is to be born at the end, the devil does not cease to persecute. WHOM RESIST, STRONG IN FAITH. Imitate therefore Christ, who overcame the devil the tempter in the desert. And note that when he says 'resist', he added 'in faith', because no virtue can lay the devil low so well as perfect faith, of which the Lord [says]: If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mountain, Move, and it would obey you.

KNOWING THAT THE SAME SUFFERING AS THAT WHICH IS IN THE WORLD IS BEFALLING YOUR BROTHERHOOD. He speaks of the same suffering in the world, namely that which the whole Church suffers. For there is no believer in the world who desires to receive the prize of eternal life and who could reach the harbour without suffering, according to what is written: Many are the tribulations of the just, and out of all these he has delivered them. And therefore, if we have been partners in the suffering, we shall also be partners in the resurrection. And elsewhere: No one will be crowned unless he has striven lawfully. And the apostle Paul: Without were fightings, within were fears. Yet the sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which will be revealed in us. BUT THE GOD OF ALL GRACE, WHO HAS CALLED US INTO HIS ETERNAL GRACE IN CHRIST JESUS, AFTER YOU HAVE SUFFERED A LITTLE. For God has called us into his eternal glory, first out of darkness into his marvellous light, because those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Yet the glory of the present time is not eternal, because it sometimes fails; of this John says: Little children, now we are sons of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. That glory is eternal which abides with God, in which the saints will go from strength to strength. And this [is] in Christ Jesus, because through the Son we have been redeemed, and through him rewarded. God the Father redeemed us through his Son, through whom he also called [us], whom he appointed to become incarnate [Codex: to be crowned] for the redemption of the human race. After you have suffered a little. He says well, 'after you have suffered a little', because the sufferings of this time are little in comparison with the blessedness to come. For thus says the Lord: Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul. HE HIMSELF WILL PERFECT, namely God, who has called us into his eternal glory; he will perfect [us] in body, WILL CONFIRM [us] in mind, WILL STRENGTHEN [us] in spirit: he will perfect in perseverance in good work, will confirm with reward, will strengthen with the prize of eternal life.
